Mr. Speaker, recently, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has received close to 1,000 letters from the residents of Geraldton, Ontario protesting their exclusion from northern tax benefits. As well, I wrote to the Minister in December with a proposal to make the current regulations fairer. To date, there has been no response from the Minister.

This mailing was taken to mean by taxpayers in the community that the Minister had changed his mind. Several residents have now mailed in their returns claiming this northern benefit. I call on the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) to take the necessary action to eliminate the confusion and to name Geraldton, Ontario as a prescribed area immediately, giving the residents the tax deduction they deserve, which they are now denied merely by being a few kilometers short of the required distance.

subtopic: S.O. 21 REFUGEES ALLEGED DISTORTION OF VOYAGE OF S.S. ST. LOUIS
S.O. 21 REFUGEES ALLEGED DISTORTION OF VOYAGE OF S.S. ST. LOUIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Members of Parliament must rely on their researchers to provide accurate information on issues they raise in the House. On February 1 and 2, two members of the NDP, speaking on Bill C-84, distorted the historical record of the tragic voyage of the S.S. St. Louis, a ship full of Jewish refugees fleeing Europe.
The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) stated, as recorded on page 15512 of Hansard, that the Canadian Government forced it to return to Europe. Further, he said that sources tell us that virtually all these people eventually met death. This is not what the historical record states.
The Canadian and American Governments communicated to the ship that it would not be allowed to disembark any of its passengers if it came to one of their ports. The ship spent its entire voyage in a Cuban port or steaming off the Florida coast. At no time did the ship even approach Canadian territorial waters.
Of the 907 people aboard the S.S. St. Louis, France took 224, Belgium took 214, Holland took 181 and Britain took 288. Of the 907, 528 escaped the Nazi Holocaust.
The St. Louis incident was a dark day for civilized society and is an example of the brutality of which mankind is capable. However, the use of history must always be exact-

Mr. Speaker, I want to call to the attention of Members of the House yet another unfair tax policy of the Tory Government. Sixty-five communities in Nova Scotia are on the qualifying list for the northern allowance, a standard tax deduction for residents of isolated areas effective for the 1987 taxation year. This deduction could mean $800 to $1,200 extra in taxpayers' pockets. Not one community in either Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick is on this qualifying list.
To make matters worse, many of the communities on the prescribed area list do not even meet the set criteria, yet they are eligible for the deductions anyway. It appears that many other maritime communities deserve this tax assistance as much as those 65 Nova Scotia communities already on the list. Why this B.C. preferential treatment? The whole matter reeks of unfairness.
The people in the western end of Prince Edward Island and elsewhere in the Maritimes deserve an explanation. I now urge
the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to give these taxpayers the explanation they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, recently, I had the privilege, as a member of the External Affairs Committee, to travel to three Middle Eastern countries at the request of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). Our purpose was to gather information and to learn more about the conflict from leaders and elected officials as well as from the people who live in the villages of the West Bank and Gaza.
As a Canadian parliamentarian, I was disappointed and frustrated in witnessing a conflict involving loss of life and human rights violations which are unacceptable, regardless of political differences.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to denounce the human rights violations which have been occurring during the past several months and to strongly support an international conference which will begin building trust and confidence between Israel and the Palestinian people.
We as Canadians pride ourselves on tolerance for each other's religious and cultural differences. While we are not perfect, I urge countries in the Middle East to follow our example.

Mr. Speaker, the livestock feed assurance program in Manitoba is failing to meet the needs of Manitoba farmers. This program is intended to insure hay production in Manitoba and is operated under the auspices of the Manitoba crop insurance program. It is funded 50 per cent by the federal Government and 50 per cent by the farmers. The province provides the administration. It is that administration which is failing the farmers.

If the program is not serving the needs of Manitoba farmers, it is not serving the needs of the federal Government.

I ask the Minister to help make sure that the interests of Manitoba farmers are well taken care of.

subsubtopic: BRANCH LINE REHABILITATION PROGRAM-INCLUSION OF BENGOUGH SUBDIVISION
speechtext:

MEECH LAKE AGREEMENT-REPORT OF SENATE TASK FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Senate task force on the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord, in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, published its report. The report makes sensible recommendations with respect to appointment mechanisms for Senators and Supreme Court judges. subsubtopic: LE DROIT-REQUEST THAT PARTIES RETURN TO NEGOTIATING TABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians residing in the National Capital Region, particularly francophones, are wondering about the future of the newspaper Le Droit whose survival is threatened should the strike last too long.
Le Droit has been the carrier of the francophone torch and the standard bearer of its cultural dissemination since 1913. We should not let this symbolic flame go out, especially here in the National Capital Region, the mirror and reflection of bilingualism in Canada, the main centre of Canadian bicultur-alism.
It would be a deplorable and even disastrous blow to information and democracy if francophone residents of the region were to lose their privileged spokesman.
This is why I strongly urge both parties in this dispute to resume negotiations in an effort to find an honourable and dignified solution, even though they may have to backtrack from their respective positions. By so doing they would preserve an essential asset of Canada's heritage.

subsubtopic: FLOW-THROUGH SHARES-REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF DECISION TO PHASE OUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question or two for the Minister of Finance. In June of last year the Minister of Finance announced, to the applause of the New Democratic Party, that he was eliminating the 33 per cent earned depletion allowance for flowthrough shares to investors in mining companies.
That may sound technical to a lot of Canadians, but it means thousands of jobs to miners in Canada. Flow-through shares have helped sustain thousands of jobs in small mining companies and small mining communities across Canada.
The Liberal Party was opposed to the Minister's decision then and is opposed to that decision now. This program was working. It was bringing hundreds of millions of dollars of investment into the mining industry. Why is the Minister phasing it out?

subsubtopic: FLOW-THROUGH SHARES-REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF DECISION TO PHASE OUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Hon. Member wanted to leave the impression that this is only being phased out on flow-through shares for small mining companies. It is being phased out for large mining companies, large oil and gas companies, as well as other players in the industry. It is being phased out in total.
The Hon. Member has asked precisely why we are making this change. It is part of the over-all balance in tax reform, part of the way in which we are reducing tax expenditures, tax breaks, and tax write-offs, as a means of broadening the tax base so that we can reduce the personal tax paid by 85 per cent of individual Canadians across Canada.
That is the substance of the reason. It is part of a broad reduction in tax expenditures, tax breaks which, as my colleague knows, have been criticized by the New Democratic Party as providing a tax write-off to wealthy investors.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been away from the House and I wanted to take the first opportunity available to me to report to Parliament upon recent events in South Africa and to discuss what Canada should do.
Canada's position in the international fight against apartheid is both important and well known. Part of our strength is that we have taken our decisions deliberately and generally kept the issue beyond the normal divisions of domestic Canadian partisanship. I report today in that spirit.
One week ago, the Government of South Africa banned political activity by 17 organizations including trade unions and the major coalition committed to non-violence. Three days
ago, it arrested peaceful marchers. Yesterday, it introduced legislation to prevent foreign funding of anti-apartheid activity and to restrict peaceful dissent still further.
Pretoria seems intent on closing the door to peaceful change. Its actions invite violence because they leave nothing else. Those actions are perverse and they are brutal. One might hope that they are designed merely for temporary electoral advantage, but we fear that they reflect a policy of deepening repression. A situation already bad has been made much worse.
In these circumstances, countries like Canada which oppose apartheid must review the nature and the effect of all our relations with South Africa. We hope that will happen in all countries that prize democracy.

Sir, the Government of Canada, guided by the Prime Minister, has played a leading role in the fight against apartheid. Our previous governments followed the line taken by Western countries. This Government is trying to orient that line. Because of our considerable interest in the African continent, our role within the Commonwealth and la Franco-phonie, and our commitment to human rights, we feel this is a question on which we can speak with authority and where we can wield some influence. We have tried to use our political and economic influence to greater effect in the fight against apartheid. We are of course disappointed in the response of the South African Government. We have also had to re-examine the need for maintaining economic and diplomatic relations with a government that seems determined to put itself above the law.
Canada's policy has been, and still is, to do everything in our power to avoid a disaster, to put an end to apartheid and to bring in a representative government that would not be based on racial divisions. The Prime Minister and I have clearly stated on many occasions that if these attempts failed, we will break off diplomatic and economic relations with South Africa. Our policy has taken various forms: economic and other sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and assistance to victims and opponents of apartheid. I would like to deal with each of these elements separately.
With respect to diplomatic relations, Sir, the choice is basic. Do we walk away in disgust or do we try to use and build our influence despite our profound disappointment? The powerful temptation is to walk away, to conclude that the South African regime is so profoundly anti-democratic that only violence will change it. Certainly the latest actions by the Pretoria Government carry South Africa away from any pretense of democracy as western nations know democracy. South Africa's apologists claim their society is part of the West. If that is so, their actions now betray their heritage.
March 2, 1988

Some Members of the House call for the end now of diplomatic relations. I wonder, with respect, whether they have considered what that would mean. For example, the South African Government has embarked upon an intensified campaign of censorship and propaganda deliberately designed to mask the reality of apartheid. Maintaining an embassy in that country is effectively the only way in which we can continue to know what is really going on. There is a value to that, and a high cost if we close.
Again, a large part of our aid program, now valued at about $5 million a year, is delivered through the embassy. Without representation on the ground it would be much more difficult to identify, supervise and monitor projects which bring real help and visible support to the victims of apartheid. Literally hundreds of small people-to-people projects, the kinds of projects we mount through our mission administered funds, literally hundreds of those projects which help the victims of apartheid in South Africa would be ended if our embassy were to close. The growing use of travel restrictions imposed upon South African opponents of apartheid means we can maintain contact with them only through our embassy. They cannot come to us, we have to go to them. We cannot do that if we are not there.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Again, in the world as it is, if we were absent from Pretoria we would have more difficulty mounting an aid program in Namibia, more difficulty advancing Canadian and Commonwealth-and I underline "and Commonwealth"-interest in South Africa, and no ability to demonstrate within South Africa itself our solidarity with anti-apartheid leaders.
The House may not know this, but whenever there is a trial on apartheid charges in South Africa accessible to our embassy, Canadian representatives are there. Whenever there is a need for solidarity with opponents of apartheid to be demonstrated physically, as when Bishop Tutu was marching three or four days ago in Pretoria, Canadian embassy representatives, the spouse of the ambassador among them, were there. Those are the kinds of things, those are the kinds of symbols that we put at risk if we close our embassy, and I ask Members who recommend that measure to consider carefully what it means.
There are countless other examples that must be considered in any serious discussion of the future of our embassy. Of course, it is valid to ask, as the Hon. Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) asked yesterday in this House, when would it be appropriate for Canada to withdraw? Sir, I do not know the answer to that question. Probably no one knows the answer to that question today. However, in all the circumstances it is the Government's considered view that this is the wrong time for Canada to walk away or cut ourselves off.

Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The issue of our economic relations is not as clear-cut. The South African Government is very anxious to maintain its economic links with the rest of the world, and is also keenly aware of its increasing isolation from the international community. Economic sanctions undoubtedly have an economic and psychological impact. The impact is even greater when sanctions are more broadly based. As 1 pointed out to the House on February 5 this year, the Commonwealth Committee of Ministers of Foreign Affairs is now gathering data and hearing recommendations that my lead to expanding, reinforcing and intensifying the application of sanction. This is becoming an increasingly urgent task, and I have already contacted my colleagues on the Committee to see how we could accelerate this program.

In addition, Sir, there are independent economic and political actions which Canada might take, including the relatively small measures for which I already have cabinet authority. Our experience is that since Canada's trade with South Africa is less than 1 per cent of South Africa's total trade, our action is more effective when it is in concert with or as catalyst to actions by nations whose economic impact is greater.
We are actively reviewing two aspects of that policy. First, to see if there are new economic measures which Canada might take effectively alone. Second, to encourage broader action, particularly by countries who prize democracy, in specific response to South Africa's multiple assaults upon freedom during the last week.
With that in mind, on the political side, we have contacted several other western Governments. Those discussions must remain confidential for the moment, but I would certainly be prepared to discuss privately with the two opposition spokesmen, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), the kind of thing we are considering in discussions with other countries.
A third focus of our activity has been upon the opponents and victims of apartheid. Their need is suddenly more urgent. The peaceful opponents of apartheid are under renewed attack. They need our assistance and we intend to provide it. We have already increased our aid for education, to the labour movement, and for humanitarian and legal aid. The challenge now is to move more money, more quickly, to the opponents and victims of apartheid.
An obvious priority is the labour movement. We provide funds to various unions in South Africa and we will provide more. Most of these funds will be channelled through the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Teachers Federation, and the Confederation des syndicats nationaux. I have instructed my officials to act urgently on precise programs submitted by those organizations.

March 2, 1988
Statements by Ministers
We will also provide new forms of assistance. For example, undoubtedly there will be challenges in court to the regulations and laws just introduced. We will take up with anti-apartheid organizations in South Africa the ways in which we would be able to help fund those court challenges.
Canada has objectives which we must pursue in support of peaceful change and dialogue. They are legitimate objectives and they are reasonable objectives. We intend to pursue them. Up until now we have been able, through our embassy, to carry out our programs in South Africa. That is why the embassy is there. If implementation of the various measures announced this past week by Pretoria prevents us from accomplishing our goals, then we will have to consider again whether our presence is justified.
The struggle in South Africa, Sir, has entered a new stage, more dangerous, more frightening. The Eminent Persons Group warned of massive bloodshed, and last week the South Africa Government pushed the region closer to that nightmare. As new rules repress opponents of apartheid within South Africa, those of us outside must become more effective and more imaginative in our initiatives. The response of Canada is particularly important because of the practical leadership we have exercised since the Nassau Conference. This is not a time for Canada to withdraw.
Quite the contrary. Our position is known and respected. What we need, indeed what I need from this House and other Canadians, are practical suggestions and initiatives that we can take, little steps and large steps, to make progress against apartheid. An interesting suggestion was made yesterday by my colleague, the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), regarding the Security Council of the United Nations, and we are examining that proposal.
We are increasing our help to the victims of apartheid, considering how we respond specifically to the Draconian new measures of last week, and we are discussing with our allies of the Commonwealth, the summit and elsewhere what new actions nations might take together.
Our Ambassador to South Africa has been back in Canada for a meeting of African Heads of Post and will be staying here a little longer for consultation. As there are new developments, I will report them to the House.
This Parliament has shown an active and nonpartisan interest in the fight against apartheid. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and I accept and exercise the Government's responsibility to lead on this issue, but naturally we would continue to be interested in practical suggestions from other Members and other Parties in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, first, 1 wish to thank the Minister for his kindness in sending me a copy of
his statement earlier today. I also wish to welcome him back to this House after being kept at home by the flu for a short time, and I hope that he is now better.
Unfortunately, there is nothing new in the statement we have just heard. I must say from the start that it certainly does not surprise me. In fact, the Minister has restated what he told this House on February 5 following the meeting of the Committee of Commonwealth Foreign Ministers in Lusaka, Zambia. Indeed, his statement that time was not that much different from what he said on November 18, 1987, when he announced the first meeting of the Committee. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Minister is working quite hard.
We do not question his good will. On the contrary, we congratulate him for his faith in the future and his determination to find a solution to apartheid through normal diplomatic channels.

We Liberals have to say that we have been frustrated over many years while in Government by this slow process which, we must say, is going absolutely nowhere. We absolutely no longer believe in it. We are of the opinion that the Botha Government cannot and will not be influenced by kid-glove diplomacy. I must add with regret that the recent actions of the Pretoria Government sustained our convictions on this side of the House.
Last week South Africa banned 18 predominantly black organizations from political activity, including the largest antiapartheid coalition and the largest labour federation. Yesterday the Government introduced legislation, the latest of a series of moves clamping down on opponents of the apartheid regime.
What we know so far of this legislation, called the Promotion of Orderly Politics Bill, is that it will prohibit all organizations from receiving money from abroad for political purposes and will empower the South African Justice Minister to seize foreign sums received by certain groups. His powers will be indefinitely retroactive. Clearly, the move could cripple antiapartheid groups and churches thus far spared from the new crack-down on opposition. Even worse, we are told that no court challenge of the restrictions would be allowed.
The Minister told us today that he urgently wants to send more money. Will the money arrive on time? Will this money have any impact under the current circumstances? Is it not too late? The clear intention of this Bill is to stop Canadian funding in South Africa. It will inevitably kill what has become one of the most visible policies in Canada's battery of attacks on the apartheid regime. Clearly, the actions of the South African Government are not aimed exclusively at Canada but certainly undermine whatever action the Canadian Government wants to take in South Africa.
We know, as the Minister certainly knows, that the trade and economic sanctions are almost fully imposed and are having little if any effect at all. The Canadian Government has
March 2, 1988

rested all of its presence in South Africa on one thing-not the sanctions, because they are not working, but on the aid that Canada could send through South Africa, reaching into South Africa to support the victims of apartheid.
We Liberals believe that as honourable as these efforts are, they are no longer, and 1 am afraid to say have probably never been, a solution. It is clear now that the Government of South Africa will never accept the introduction of non-racial representative governments. Unless bold action is taken, the diplomatic soft glove approach will never succeed.
I submit that the Pretoria Government has made a declaration of war on peace, justice, and human rights. We are now, more than ever, in a position to cut our relations there. The time has come to do it in the face of what has been taking place in South Africa.
The Minister may have genuine aspirations, but I submit that his declaration is a repetition of a number of things which have been said in the past and it will not work. When the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) spoke at the United Nations he got applause and praise, not because of his effort there but because he said that he was ready soon to cut diplomatic relations with South Africa. That is when he got the applause.
I regret very much the Minister's portrayal of our suggestions of breaking diplomatic relations as walking away, as cutting ourselves off from this problem. This is not true. This is not what we have been saying and it is certainly not the view of the Liberal Party of Canada which has been constantly, for many years, against apartheid and continues to be against apartheid. We continue to be against apartheid. But we want to venture into new avenues to find a breakthrough in this area.
We have never said and are not saying that the Government should stop its actions within the Commonwealth. We have never said and will never say that the Government should stop supporting the South African Development Co-ordinating Conference.
Canada could show leadership by breaking relations with South Africa, bringing about the realization once and for all that there is no future in trying to convince the Botha Government through the diplomatic route.

Canada will host the next Economic Summit in Toronto, next June. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should use this opportunity to convince his allies to apply real economic pressures in an effort to weaken the will of the Pretoria Government.
I believe that the Minister can and should continue his work with the Commonwealth Foreign Ministers but to do so, he does not have to maintain diplomatic relations with South Africa.
Statements by Ministers

He said in his remarks that the question of economic relations is less clear-cut. The South African Government is extremely sensitive to both its economic link with the world and its growing isolation in the international community. Economic sanctions undoubtedly have an impact economically and psychologically. That impact is greater when those sanctions are more broadly supported.

This is what we are saying. The Government must initiate talks with the United States and the member countries of the Group of Seven, which could impose strong enough economic sanctions to make the South African Government change its position.
I was suprised that the Minister did not refer to the comments of the Secretary General of the Commonwealth, who proposed yesterday a five-point plan which should receive our enthusiastic support. The Secretary of the Commonwealth said the following:

"A widening, tightening and intensification of economic and other sanctions should be imposed by the United Nations". We support that. Second: "Increased pressure by Third World countries on those western countries that have not imposed tough economic sanctions". This is a route to follow.
Third: "A ban by black-ruled African countries on the use of their air space by airlines flying to South Africa". That is another proposal that should be very carefully considered and implemented.
Finally: "A concerted international demand on the Botha Government to enter into power-sharing negotiations with South Africa's black majority". Clearly, this demand will not be answered by the Botha Government unless countries like Canada are prepared to take bold initiatives. One of those initiatives is for us to show the lead and cut our ties.
I note that our ambassador is now in Ottawa and that the Minister said he wants to retain him for further consultations. I suggest that he should retain him as long as possible. In other words, until the Botha Government has not begun talking with the black leaders of South Africa to share authority in government in South Africa.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by thanking the Minister for reporting to the House. We are glad to have him back on his feet after his having been confined to bed for the last week or so. I must say that we have missed him due to the many questions we would have liked to ask him. We will try to make up for that in the coming weeks.
The Minister began his statement by saying that he reports in the spirit of nonpartisanship which has attended this issue. While that is certainly the case with respect to the mutual and commonly felt abhorrence of all Canadians and Members of Parliament toward the apartheid regime in South Africa, I

March 2, 1988
Statements by Ministers
hope the Minister will also respect the fact that within the boundaries of that nonpartisanship there is room for honest and profound disagreement about the appropriate Canadian response to that issue. It is in that spirit that I, on behalf of my Party, offer our criticisms of the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark).
I honestly believe that the measured tone and lack of new initiative today does not do justice to the fundamental objections Canadians have expressed to the actions taken by the South African Government in recent days. When one considers the obvious slap in the face given to the Minister and his colleagues in Lusaka recently by the South African Government, basically ignoring the Commonwealth group, it seems that the Minister spoke more calmly than might have been in order. The South African Government has made it clear that it does not really care about what the Minister and other Commonwealth leaders think. It has basically told them to get lost.
1 suggest the time has come not only for action but for more passion in the response of the Canadian Government to what has happened in South Africa.
Nothing could be more offensive to me and, I am sure, to many others than knowing that South Africa permits neo-Nazis to march down the street without government harassment while, only days later, Bishop Tutu, Reverend Boesak and other leaders in the Christian community are arrested for a peaceful demonstration against apartheid. As a Christian myself, 1 am sure all Canadians, Christian and non Christian, feel the same repugnance at this obvious affront to democratic principles, freedom of speech, and the very possibility of nonviolent action against apartheid in South Africa.
The approach taken by the Minister in his statement suggests a certain innocence. I am not sure whether it is a studied innocence, or a naive innocence, but it is there. For instance, he acknowledged that only yesterday it was announced there would be legislation to prevent foreign funding of anti-apartheid activity, yet later in his statement he talked at great length about how the Canadian Government intends to step up its support of anti-apartheid activity in South Africa through the Canadian Labour Congress and various other avenues open to the Canadian Government. Does the Minister not see that this declaration of war on peace and justice that the Liberal spokesman referred to is also a declaration of war on Canada's anti-apartheid activity? Some of the Minister's own officials have implied that this legislation may indeed be targeted at Canada. Perhaps it would have been appropriate for the Minister to respond to that and indicate how the Canadian Government intends to overcome the obvious intention of the South African Government to frustrate the very policies on which the Minister states the Government will now put even more emphasis.
Not only are the Front Line States that are opposed to apartheid in South Africa to be harassed, those in Canada and
other parts of the world who choose to actively support antiapartheid groups in South Africa are to be harassed as well.
The Minister says that as a result of recent events, South Africa policy is under review. I would have thought that the Department of External Affairs would have had at least anticipated that something like this might happen some day. It might have had a contingency response available so that when the South African Government did act in the way it has, Canadian action could have been swift. It could be shown that we do not have to dither over our response to this kind of action. Unfortunately, that is not the case.
It seems to me and my colleagues that the Minister, at the very least, could have proceeded-and we realize this is a significant action, but significant events are taking place which call for a significant response-to announce a Canadian policy of mandatory and comprehensive economic sanctions against South Africa. That would have been a clear response on behalf of Canada. That would have been in concert, I believe, with the level of concern all Canadians feel about apartheid in South Africa.
We might constitute 1 per cent of trade with South Africa, but we are not talking about a statistical reality, we are talking about a political reality, a symbolic reality and a moral reality. Whether it is 1 per cent, 10 per cent or 40 per cent, in the final analysis it does not matter that much.
With respect to the question of diplomatic relations, the position of the New Democratic Party is different from that of the Liberal Party. We accept some of the arguments made by the Minister for maintaining some kind of diplomatic presence in South Africa. However, we certainly take the view that the time has come for a downgrading of our diplomatic recognition of South Africa. The opportunity presents itself because the ambassador is here in Canada. It is certainly an opportunity for the Minister to discuss with the ambassador how that might be done. I believe we have to take action both on the economic and the diplomatic front. I would recommend that to the Minister. Other avenues which are available on the diplomatic front are things we suggested yesterday, having to do with the United Nations and the Security Council. We hope some of those avenues might be constructively pursued.
With respect to the question of breaking off diplomatic relations, I say to the Minister that I believe what he has found frustrating about the current debate is due in part to the repeated assertions by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that this is something that Canada is prepared to do, and not in some far away mythological time, but a very real possibility under certain circumstances. The call from some quarters for a break-off in diplomatic relations is attributable in part to the Prime Minister repeatedly mentioning this as a possible Canadian response when the time comes. As to that time, 1 agree with the Minister that it is never possible to know when that time is.
March 2, 1988

With respect to economic sanctions, I think sometimes there is a tendency to talk about them without anyone actually elucidating exactly what that would involve. What do we export to South Africa? I am told, having checked with the Interchurch Task Force on Corporate Responsibility, that one of our major exports to South Africa is sulphur. In 1986, the last year for which statistics are available, sulphur made up some 39 per cent of our exports to South Africa. This is one step the Government could take if it were to impose mandatory sanctions. The sulphur that goes to South Africa is used to make fertilizer which is, in turn, sold to the Front Line States. It has been suggested, I am told, that instead of being exported to South Africa, this sulphur could be exported to the Front Line States as part of an aid project and they could begin to make their own fertilizer with the sulphur, which would have the double effect of instituting both sanctions and less dependency by the Front Line States on South Africa. This proposal, 1 understand, is only in the embryonic stage, but 1 suggest to the Minister that it is a course of action which should be looked into.
We export small amounts of many other things to South Africa, potash from Saskatchewan, wheat, wood pulp, mining machinery and man-made fibres from Ontario, tungsten from British Columbia, folding cardboard boxes from Quebec. All these things, of course, are not going to break the back of the South African Government, but that is not the point. We want the Government to show leadership, to act, not just on behalf of Canadians but on behalf of all the people of the world who are concerned about apartheid, by taking these kinds of actions. We think that would have the effect of making it more possible, not less possible, for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to get the kind of widespread co-operatively decided upon sanctions to which he so often refers.
I ask the Minister what he means when he talks in his statement about sanctions being more broadly supported. Is he hopeful we can bring the United States, and Britain in particular, on side in more decisive action? Perhaps that is the kind of thing he intends to let us in on if we take him up on his offer to have meetings. I can say now that we are open to having those kind of consultations and we appreciate the offer.
Finally, I feel, and 1 think my colleagues also feel, that there is something far too gentle about this response on the part of the Canadian Government. Today was a day in which history could have been made in terms of a Canadian response to apartheid in South Africa. Instead, the Minister has persisted in his policy. I think it is a policy he sincerely holds, but nevertheless it is a policy that is starting to undermine, in my judgment, the well-deserved reputation of the Prime Minister and the Minister with respect to apartheid. I believe the leadership they have shown has arisen out of a genuine sincerity with respect to this issue. It has not been a political tactic. However, I think the time has come for some form of action to be taken by Canada by itself. It could have happened today and it did not. We regret that. However, we offer to

Mr. Speaker, 1 also have the pleasure to present another petition from a number of constituents regarding the trade deal with the United States. They believe that the federal Government lacks a mandate from the people of Canada to conclude this type of a trade deal with the United States.
They believe that this trade deal threatens the very fabric of our Canadian political and economic sovereignty since it removes the power of the Canadian Government to control foreign ownership.
They believe that it would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and thereby undermine our ability to build a distinct society from that of the United States of America.
They are asking Parliament now to dissolve to enable the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade deal during a national general election.

Mr. Speaker, the petition I present is duly certified and concerns the trade agreement that the Government has negotiated with the United States.
The petitioners point out that the Government had no mandate to negotiate such an agreement and that in the course of the negotiations Canadian sovereignty was compromised, something which it was specifically promised would not happen. The trade agreement threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty. It removes our ability to control foreign ownership and to develop or to equalize opportunities between the regions.
Therefore the petitioners call upon Parliament to dissolve and to allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade agreement during a national general election.

maintopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 BILL C-109-CHANGE IN REFERENCE OF BILL

Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions to present. One is from a number of residents in Burnaby, North Vancouver, Maple Ridge and Salish Court. These people are concerned about the trade deal signed between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States without any mandate from the Canadian people and in spite of a promise by the Prime Minister not to compromise Canadian sovereignty.
They point out that it completely fails to win secure access to the United States markets, which was the stated goal, and that it risks losing hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs and that it would deny to Canada the freedom to choose policies that would direct our own future. In fact, it undermines our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
Therefore, they pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and to allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have another petition from the residents of Spadina in which they remind Parliament that in February of 1985 the Government directed the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to prepare a report on equality rights in Canada.
March 2, 1988

The committee duly reported to the House and, among other things, recommended that the Human Rights Act be amended to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in all areas under federal jurisdiction, including the RCMP, the Canadian Armed Forces and the age of consent legislation with regard to sexual orientation and practice.
They point out that the Government subsequently promised to take whatever measures are necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination but that the Government has not yet taken any significant action in this direction. Therefore they request Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament act to implement the recommendations contained in the report as specified above with all due haste and speed, as in duty bound your petitioners will ever pray.

speechtext:
Considerable progress has been made toward a new standard for the National Flag for outdoor use (long-term).
The Canadian General Standards Board, lacking any regulatory authority, is not in a position to bring into effect all the provisions of the cited Act. At the present time it can only proceed with the development of a new National Standard of Canada to reflect current manufacturing techniques and materials.
Since the passage of the National Flag of Canada Manufacturing Standards Act, the representative CGSB Standards Committee has been reactivated to develop a new edition of the existing National Standard on the National Flag using the consensus process.
The Standards Committee identified the problem with the red portions of the flag and subsequent testing was necessary to eveluate various dyes and fabrics. It was agreed to expose various test flags on a continuous basis to conditions of actual use in the Toronto area. This testing was done by a private testing organization and was completed in December, 1987, and a report is expected by the end of February, 1988. The report will then be circulated to all members of the Committee and a meeting scheduled to prepare the revised standard. It is expected that the final standard for outdoor long-term flags will be available for the end of 1988.

speechtext: I wish to inform the House that, because of the ministerial statement, Government Orders will be extended by 39 minutes. The Hon. Member for Yorkton- Melville (Mr. Nystrom).

The House resumed from March 1 consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of Western Canada, to establish the Department of Western Economic Diversification and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House today is Bill C-113. It is a Bill which is very important in principle to establish a western diversification department and diversification offices across western Canada to try to diversify the economy.
The idea itself is very sound in principle in terms of diversification. It is very sound in terms of more decentralization in western Canada in bringing decision-making closer to the people. The question is, why should we diversify in the West? It is very important that we do so, because the economy of western Canada is extremely dependent upon resources, on one hand, and agriculture on the other hand. In both those cases, we are dependent upon the cyclical pricing nature of those commodities. The economy of western Canada depends a lot on what is happening in the New York stock market, the metal market, the commodity market in Chicago, or the international grain price. When things are going badly internationally, the price that the producer receives in western Canada goes down. That affects the entire economy. It has negative spinoffs, and a negative effect on jobs. Therefore, it is very important that there be some way of diversifying the economy of western Canada.
One of the concerns that I have, as do members of the general population in the West, is that the Government is not putting up very much money in terms of western diversification. Here we have $1.2 billion to be spent in four provinces over five years, which is some $60 million per year, per province, in western Canada.
In 1980 the former Liberal Government was criticized by the Conservatives across the way when it established the Western Development Fund of $4 billion over four years. That
was a little more money, and much of that money did not seem to appear either. It seemed to be a phantom fund. If the Government does not want to turn people off in western Canada, it is very important that there be some real money and funding of western Canadian diversification.
There are other areas where the Government could be doing more in terms of helping western Canadians. One area is procurement. I remember year after year Conservatives criticizing former Liberal Governments for not buying enough in western Canada and purchasing too many goods and services in Ontario and in Quebec, particularly in the Ottawa region of Ontario.
I have statistics here that are very interesting in terms of procurement of goods and services in western Canada. In 1981-82 in the four western provinces the federal Government purchased some 15.5 per cent of its supplies. The Department of Supply and Services contracts on a dollar basis in terms of western Canada indicate that 15.5 per cent of supplies were purchased in western Canada in 1981-82. By the time the Conservative Government took office in 1984, only 13.9 per cent of supplies were purchased in western Canada. The following year that went down to 12.8 per cent. Last year, in 1986-87, it went down to 11.5 per cent.
The Conservative Government claims to be very sensitive about the West. It has a lot of western representation and powerful Ministers from western Canada, for example, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), the Minister of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn). Yet only 11.5 per cent of its purchasing is in western Canada. When the Government took office it was 13.9 per cent.
I suggest that this is one area where a lot more jobs could be created in western Canada if there were some regional equity in terms of the purchasing policy of the Government of Canada. Western Canada has approximately 27 or 28 per cent of the population, and the Government only purchases 11.5 per cent of its goods and services there.
Some people say it is because the West is so far away from Ottawa; it is too far away from the federal Government. I do not buy that. There are many government agencies in western Canada. There is much federal Government activity in western Canada. Western Canada has many service industries, and much of the purchasing could occur right in the West. The major point I make is that, not only is it 11.5 per cent of the share, but that share has gone down from 15.5 per cent in 1981-82, so there has been a sharp drop-off.
I notice there is a very influential Minister present who is in charge of the Treasury Board. Perhaps he could have some influence on those particular purchasing policies. The Minister is shaking his head in the negative.

I have not been President of the Treasury Board for six months. Wake up!
March 2, 1988

Ele is no longer President of the Treasury Board. Well, we did not notice the impact over here, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps he could have some influence on the purchasing policies of the Government, because he is a very influential Minister.
I understand that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazan-kowski) is now in charge of the Treasury Board. We find that this has not helped. Here we have a western Minister and there is still this procurement policy of the Government where it is discriminating against western Canada. Members of the Government sit back and laugh about this discrimination against western Canada. It is no wonder that the Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) left that caucus and denounced the Government on its procurement policy in terms of lack of purchases in western Canada.
The second point I wish to make is in terms of the spending of the federal Government. Since this bunch of clowns took office three years ago, spending on regional development went down by some $3 billion. This Government stated that it would do a lot more in terms of spending in western Canada, spending in the North, and helping people in depressed regions. Yet less and less money is being spent in western Canada in terms of regional economic development than was spent before. The latest public opinion polls indicate that the current Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is even less popular in western Canada than was Pierre Trudeau. No wonder. There has been a tremendous betrayal of the people of western Canada.
In a Government study it indicates that, in the last 25 years, federal government expenditures in regional development have been approximately 3 per cent of the Government of Canada's economic expenditures. That is a very small amount. The Macdonald Royal Commission on Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada stated that a lot more must be done in terms of spending in regional development in Canada. They stated, "The Commission believes that regional development must remain an essential component of Canadian policy". The report further stated, "We recommend a new federal-provincial system of sharing regional development expenditures and responsibilities". The report also stated that they must have the insurance that there be a high level of infrastructural support.
The report goes on, and 1 wish to quote one further statement: "The Commissioners believe that the total federal financial commitment to regional development, combining of regional economic development grants and other funds spent through ERDAs should be increased significantly over the next two years".
This commission headed by Mr. Macdonald spent millions of dollars doing economic research in this country. They made recommendations that there be an increase in the spending on regional development in this country over the next few years. Yet the Conservative Party has been cutting back, cutting back, and cutting back on the amount of money it is spending
Western Economic Diversification Act
on regional development. I suggest once again that that is not fair, in the same manner as it is very unfair to be spending less and less on government procurement throughout the West.
Another point I would like to make in terms of western diversification is that we are going to have to diversify more from depending only on resources, fisheries, agriculture, and things of that type and diversify into high technology, advanced technology, and things of that nature. It is interesting to note that the OECD was asked by the four western provinces to conduct a study of innovation policy in western Canada. The OECD study team was in the West in the fall of 1985. Their report was released in early 1987. In that report they stated that the expenditure in terms of research and development in Canada as a whole is very low. The expenditure in western Canada is even lower. More funding should go to universities, industries, and fields such as biotechnology, electronics, telecommunications, and computer software. This study was commissioned by the four western provinces.
There are a number of other things that could be said about the importance of diversifying the economy in western Canada. Last spring our Party decided to spend some time in attempting to come up with a number of suggestions for the Government. We released a text of a western economic diversification statement in July. At that time we talked about the importance of diversifying the economy in the West. We started off by saying it was important to build on what we had. We have a very strong resource economy. We have all kinds of natural resources, gas, oil, potash, iron ore, things of that sort on which we should be building. Second, we should build on the very strong agricultural economy in western Canada as well as the very strong fishing and lumber economy located in the Province of British Columbia. We believe as a Party that a focus on diversification should involve as much regional and local control as possible where farmers and fishermen in the western towns, villages and cities have as much input as possible over decisions that affect their development and lives.
In the past we have had too many top heavy programs planned from Ottawa which have had little local input from local folks. Third, we suggested that more emphasis be put on small and medium-sized enterprises. All too often Governments rely on megaprojects and on spending money to subsidize large corporations, many of which are foreign and, again, all the requisite statistics will show that the smaller and medium-sized companies tend to be the ones which produce jobs, have more impact and give a lot more bang for the buck.
A lot of value could be added to our western resources. There are all kinds of jobs we are not getting because we tend to export many raw materials from western Canada without any processing, upgrading or some value added before exporting resources to other countries, primarily the United States.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
We could create jobs in western Canada by servicing the needs of our resource industries. We have a great forest industry and yet the majority of the equipment for the forest industry is imported rather than produced in Canada. We have a mining industry in the West, but most of the mining machinery is imported rather than produced in western Canada. There is a tremendous amount of agriculture and farming in western Canada and, again, farm machinery is imported in the main rather than being produced in the West. A major reason is that we have free trade in farm machinery implements in western Canada and because of that we have lost our basic industry, most therefore is produced elsewhere, and we lose jobs and economic spin-offs.
We believe there is the possibility of developing some manufacturing industry in western Canada. In our paper we gave some examples of what can be done in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia. Finally, there is the creation of new jobs in new industries, specifically advanced and high technology, where we should be diversifying. In places like Saskatoon we have some high technology industries that are doing very well, but we believe we could be doing a lot more work in that area right across the West.
What about the whole area of services? There are all kinds of service industries today creating many jobs. Then we have tourism. Tourism in the West could be promoted more than it is today, although we have been helped recently by the Calgary Olympics and by Expo 86 in the City of Vancouver.
Finally there is trade diversification. Since this Government has taken power a tremendous amount of time has been spent on a trade deal with the United State. A lot more emphasis could be put on trying to diversify our trade with other countries around the world. I noticed the positive statement in the press by the Minister for International Trade about being more aggressive in trading with Hong Kong as Hong Kong becomes part of China. We need to be doing more in China, which has a population of one billion people. The Pacific Rim is very important.
The United States is not quite as relevant to trade within western Canada as it is with Canada as a whole. The United States is still our number one trading partner and always will be. But in western Canada, in Saskatchewan in particular, other countries are important to us. The Chinese are important to Saskatchewan for grain sales and potash, but other Pacific countries are important also to the Province of Saskatchewan.
There are a number of other points that could be made, but I want to conclude by saying that we certainly support the principles of the Bill to establish a new department of diversification in western Canada. The important thing is for this department to have a sufficient supply of money to do a really meaningful and effective job. Some of the money the Government is now spending of the SI.2 billion is not new money. It is old money from other Departments recycled into a new department, a department of western diversification. One reason is to give it a higher profile to enhance the Conservative
Party's election opportunities. I say that because if it turns out to be the case, there will be more cynicism and more alienation in the West and more and more people will be looking for more and more radical options, something we cannot afford to play around with. At the moment we do not have very much support for western separatist Parties. That being said, there is still a great feeling of alienation in western Canada. The Western Canada Concept still exists, the Confederation of Regions Party still exists. It would not take much more to start fanning the flames of western independence and western separatism again. I urge the Government to put more money into this department, try to diversify the economy of the West and do something meaningful and creative to make those of us in western Canada feel that we are fully 100 per cent part of the great Canadian Confederation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to stand in the House today to contribute to this debate. I will attempt to keep my remarks relatively brief in the hope that opposition Party Members might also keep their remarks brief so we can move this legislation forward to committee, through the process, and have it in place as quickly as possible because it has been a long time in coming.
I was elected to this Chamber in May, 1979. I have felt for a very long time that the regions of Canada were sufficiently diverse. Instead of a centralized type of program which characterized the Liberal-NDP years control of this country I felt that we needed initiatives specifically related to the regions which might serve the needs of the people.
It is particularly interesting to hear the Member opposite as the first speaker for the New Democratic Party on this issue. He is a westerner. Our roots are not dissimilar, but I would like to make it very clear to the Chamber that the kinds of ideas we have about what is right and wrong in Canada and what needs to be changed arise from perhaps very different philosophical roots. I hear the Member opposite and I hear Members of his Party rather consistently saying, "We will stand up for the west".
Which we do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is the sort of thing that comes from the right-hand side of their mouths. But what about the left hand side of their mouths, Mr. Speaker? In 1979 we had a Government elected in Canada with a very strong western representation with a Prime Minister from the West. At the first available opportunity the NDP passed a motion in the House supported by the Liberals and threw the Government out of office. After so many years of lack of western representation, the New Democrats threw us out of office. We were left with four and a half close to five years of government with only two western Members sitting on the government benches and only one in Cabinet.
March 2, 1988

What happened to the West? In my city, the unemployment rate went from 3.5 per cent to 12.7 per cent because of federal government policies oriented toward central Canada by a Government that perhaps knew no better, a Government supported in the assumption of office, in the first instance and continuously, by the New Democratic Party.
What has happened since then? We finally have a Government with the strongest cabinet representation from western Canada in the history of the country. We have a Government that is committed to addressing in turn each and every major grievance that has existed since the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan joined Confederation.
As we bring forward statutes and programs that are absolutely vital and necessary to the diversification and strength of the western economy, time after time we get filibusters and fighting in the House. At the centre of that tactic is the slowing down of public policy initiatives required by the West. At the centre of the strategy designed to thwart and subvert those positive actions, we find the members of the New Democratic Party. They say out of the right sides of their mouths that they care about western Canada and out of the left sides of their mouths and the actions they take in this Chamber that they are dedicated time after time to stopping the progress of the West dead in its tracks.
Every day I sit through petitions and listen to petition after petition after petition coming from NDP riding associations in western Canada. These petitions say that we should get rid of the trade agreement. I would expect that point of view to come from the mouths of the most powerful union leaders in the country who live in central Canada. They like to control the supply while the benefits to their members rise higher. Members from western Canada have become captives of those labour leaders of the powerful unions. To use this House to advance the interests of those people at the expense of western Canadians is unconscionable.
There is not one reputable economist in Canada who does not believe that the trade deal will be good for Canada and for the young people of Canada. The economists go one step further. They tell us consistently that it will be especially good for western Canada.
The Hon. Member has the gall to say that we need value added to the resources of western Canada. To that extent, he is right. We do need value added to the things we produce, but we have to sell them somewhere. To have the jobs, the factories, the plants and the processing, we have to have a market. That market is indeed the entire world, but if we are to serve the entire world on a competitive basis, we need the economies of scale and we need the investments. Someone has to come up with the money to build the processing plants and the factories. Someone has to come up with the money to market the products. To be competitive in the market-place, we need to have access to the markets.
Western Economic Diversification Act
If the Hon. Member had one bit of interest in history, he could study a number of occasions since World War II on which small nations entered into trading arrangements with larger nations and increased their market potential. In each and every single instance, the smaller nation benefited by increased jobs, more satisfying jobs, better paying jobs and increased standards of living for the entire nation. That is what history since World War II has told us and that is what the economists are telling us will happen to Canada and in particular western Canada. Day after day, members of the New Democratic Party fight that vital initiative for western Canada.
Did members of the NDP support FIRA, the Foreign Investment Review Agency, which we changed? They supported FIRA. The Hon. Member smiles with pride and-
It wasn't strong enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He says that it was not strong enough. As a consequence of FIRA, Canadian investment left the country and foreign investment stopped coming in. There were well over 1.5 million unemployed Canadians within a very brief period of time.
This Government said that the philosophy of FIRA was wrong and needed to be changed. We wanted an agency called Investment Canada which would encourage Canadians and others to invest in this country. Members of the NDP said that we were wrong and that the Minister of Finance's Budgets were wrong. They said that we would increase the unemployment rolls.
I would like Canadians to recall those early days in the fall of 1984 and the spring of 1985. Members of the NDP said that if we changed FIRA and put in a Budget that encouraged investment, we would produce more unemployed Canadians. That is the logical chain in the belief system of members of the Opposition and particularly members of the New Democratic Party. What happened, though? Canadians are better off today. Over 1,100,000 more jobs have been created, 85 per cent of which are full-time jobs, as a consequence of economic attitudes on the part of Conservative Members that have produced and built upon the individual initiative of individual Canadians.
We believe in a system that challenges individual Canadians to be energetic, to take risks and to succeed. If we do that and if we do it well, it works.
What would NDP Members replace that with? They would replace it with a system of more civil servants, more decisionmakers employed by Government, higher costs to individual taxpayers and less freedom for individuals. Their policies take us consistently in that direction. Surely Canadians have had enough experience with that to know that it leads inevitably to higher unemployment, more tragedy, more wife beating, more suicide and more of all of the social consequences which they profess to wish to avoid.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Members of the NDP should look back in time just a bit. The two NDP Members opposite were here when the Government increasingly intervened in the lives of people with things like the National Energy Program. They saw the consequences for Canadians and yet they did not seem to learn. It is as if there were a genetic reason right from the beginning that they have to hold on to a belief system, no matter how antiquated or how inefficient it is, simply because they have always believed it. There seems to be an inability to learn from experience.
What are we doing? Canada's patent legislation was out of step. They supported that initiative long before these Members came along. Members on our side said that when you do that, your commitment to research and development will decline, jobs in that field will decline, your standard of living will decline, and your employment rate will decline. They would not listen, they would not learn, and it all came about. Our research and development declined. Young Canadians with skills, talent and energy had to leave the country to find jobs in R and D.
After watching it for 15 years, and watching these things come to pass, this Government brought in initiatives to change that, and all we got was a filibuster. We were delayed in passing that legislation for well over a year. It is a job-creating initiative that will help western Canada, central Canada, and Atlantic Canada but the Opposition fought it.
What have they done on immigration? Each day the social welfare case-load in Canada grows through illegal, unplanned immigration. Each day that happens, money is paid out. Taxpayers have paid out hundreds of millions of dollars. The law we inherited did not allow determinations to be made in any kind of efficient manner. It invited illegal migrant flows, people who by no stretch of the imagination could be classified by anyone as refugees, coming as they did in large numbers from western democratic countries. Yet the Opposition refuses to allow sensible legislation to pass the Chamber.
In 1988 alone the Opposition has spent six days of the House of Commons time filibustering some simple amendments from the Senate. We could have been talking about regional diversity and the western diversification program, topics essential to the well-being of this nation. Instead the Opposition chooses to filibuster refugee legislation for six days.
Then we come to a budget and the need to borrow money. In the six days of budget debate we got very few kudos for reducing the Government's borrowing requirements and saving future generations some of the load. Then we find out that in those six days of debate the Opposition did not learn enough about the need for borrowing, so we got two and a half more days of debate on a borrowing Bill. Close to nine full days were spent on the economy with no useful suggestions. There was just a lot of political posturing while legislation piles up.
Did we get any help on tackling the long-term western Canadian grievance on transportation? The Opposition stalled
two pieces of legislation day after day after day. They would have provided a better sense of equity to western Canadians in the transportation field. Absolutely fundamental changes were required to enable the western economy to grow, develop and diversify, yet what do we get from the NDP? Filibuster. Filibuster. Stall. Filibuster. Filibuster. Why? Do they value the myth of power so highly that any behaviour is justified in the pursuit of that power?
Is there a single piece of evidence in the three and a half years of this Parliament of consistently helpful behaviour by the Opposition? We just get rhetoric. We get rhetoric by the carload. It would be nice if we could weigh the rhetoric to give you some sense of how large it is getting. It would completely dwarf any sense-

Point of order, Mr. Speaker. I hate to interrupt a veteran Member, although you would never know he was, but there is a rule of relevance. He should be speaking to what is in the Bill before the House instead of everything else he has been throwing up before us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the shoe must be pinching just a little because so much truth is being laid on the table.
The Hon. Member referred to tourism. Western diversification relates to tourism. Is there any credit for the very early decision taken by this Government to spend several million dollars in a new advertising campaign consisting of television and radio commercials?
Pittance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Hon. Member says it is a pittance.
You bet it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If tourism is up in western Canada by 35 per cent or 40 per cent, how many jobs for real people who need a real income does that represent? Yet the Member shouts "pittance". Governments he supported for so many years did not spend that pittance. They did not create those jobs. This Government did.
What did they do on energy? They invented a grand scheme involving PIP grants to the oil industry. Now we see the court cases involving abuses of those grants. We rang the bells for 17 days in this Chamber and then we had a committee process.
Are you proud of that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was there every hour of every day telling government Members the consequences of that program, how many lives would be ruined as a consequence. I told them what would happen to the economy. This would increase suicides, spouse and child battering. Yet I did not see the NDP, sitting alongside me in those committee meetings, fighting for the people of western Canada. I do not see them in this Chamber today fighting for the people of western Canada. I expect what we will see through the balance of this day, into tomorrow and the next day this is debated, is NDP Members from western
March 2, 1988

Canada filibustering the western diversification fund. How in God's name they can translate that kind of tactic into something useful for western Canadians is beyond my wildest imagination.
Statutory legislative authority to produce a mechanism and fund unbounded by central Canadian dictates but open to the flavour of the West, the creativity of the West, is what we are creating in this legislation. Our part of Canada is as unique as Quebec. It is as unique as Newfoundland. That is part of the charm of Canada. This Government believes that unique programs and practices are required in the different regions. As western Canadians, some born in western Canada, they should know that reality and be supportive of our efforts to achieve that result.
Let us watch what the NDP does. Do they facilitate or block an initiative designed to help western Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my hon. friend. My recollection is that we have been debating this Bill for about three or four hours and he is already calling it a filibuster. I realize that this is one of the Members who stormed the Chair of the House of Commons. He broke all parliamentary tradition by shutting down the House of Commons, standing before the Speaker, shaking his fist and screaming. They held this House to ransom day after day after day. Some of us were sickened at that behaviour. Presumably the Hon. Member is proud of the fact that he was prepared to strangle the voice of this House, throttle debate, and essentially close this House and Parliament down.
I was not pleased with that. I was not proud of that. I was embarrassed by the fact that the Hon. Member and his colleagues decided that was an appropriate tactic. That is dictatorial. It is something we would find in a fascist system and certainly has no place in a parliamentary democracy.
Having said that, my hon. colleague from Yorkton- Melville indicated that sourcing of supplies and services is one way the federal Government can assist the local manufacturing economy, particularly that in western Canada. Yet the statistics are very clear that government sourcing in western Canada has decreased over the last four years. There is less government sourcing in western Canada on a percentage basis than ever before. Eighty per cent of federal government sourcing continues to be from isolated portions of central Canada.
How does the Member explain the Government's interest in western Canada if it is sourcing less of its goods and services from the West, on a percentage basis, than ever before? Second, does he really believe that after three or four hours of debate on a very important issue with regard to the diversification of the western Canadian economy we have debated for too long, that the debate should stop, and that anything further would be considered a filibuster?
Western Economic Diversification Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, every time opposition Members open their mouths they give us lots of things to say. One of the tragedies of this Chamber is the lack of thorough research in the Opposition. I particularly resent a person of the Member's stature within his Party saying that I stormed the Chair. I never did. I never have. I care deeply about the Constitution of Canada and I participated actively in the committee hearings from morning until midnight. I cared about it in the Chamber and I stood in my place and participated in the filibuster, which was the longest in parliamentary history, because it was a fundamental issue to the people of this country, but I did not storm the Chair. I did not break the rules. I think the Member's research should be better founded in this case and in many others.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I did imply that the Hon. Member was one of the group which stormed the Speaker's chair. I simply assumed that due to his enthusiastic support of that initiative he would have been a member of that group. However, if he was not part of the group that stormed the Chair and closed down Parliament for a number of days, I will retract that and apologize to my hon. friend. I would not like to link him with the group which carried out that particular act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that comment. I participated in two filibusters in this Chamber. One was the ringing of the bells and the consequences of that which was related to the energy Bills.
In terms of the Constitution, I believed that my part of the country would be forced to leave Canada if the original version of that had passed. It would have shoved me out of my own country. I worked with Members of the Opposition, including the one who spoke before me, to ensure that the original version did not pass and we succeeded. We can stay in Canada with pride.
Second, I participated in the filibuster on the energy Bills because they were going to devastate western Canada, my city in particular, and to some extent the entire country. They were wrong-headed and wrongly drafted. We did not succeed, and that is a tragedy. I look at the anguish in my community day after day and wish I had somehow been able to avoid it.
Those are two fundamental issues and it is the responsibility of people in this Chamber to filibuster, to fight, and to use all the tools available on fundamental issues. However, it is a travesty that the reality of this place is that pieces of legislation are filibustered which deserve to be passed through the House into committee for detailed study and to be reported back. To plug up the legislative agenda on things like copyright, immigration, and western diversification is not the proper use of this Chamber or of taxpayers' funds. This place was not invented for that purpose.
In Britain, the mother of Parliaments, most legislation is debated in the House for less than a day. It is very rare that it takes more than a day. Yet in this Chamber we are exposed to

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
blocking tactics. If the Opposition wants to block positive initiatives such as western diversification, let us take it to the voters. Let us lay out the record of blockage on initiatives that are helpful to western Canadians.
Call an election tomorrow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let us go to an election and explain to western Canadians what we have done with regard to reorienting the system of government to give all regions of the country a say in decision making. Let us take to the voters a piece of legislation such as this which so clearly says that western culture will be attended to and decisions will be made in western Canada. The program is flexible to encompass the aspirations of people who live in that region. Let us go to the voters and tell them that the NDP will say one thing but will do another.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Member from Calgary is living in dreamland. He is talking about filibusters and so on. I have been here for many years and have seen his Party in opposition. If there was a Party that was expert at filibustering and delaying, it was the Conservative Party in opposition.
