One need only think of people like Erik Nielsen to think of filibusters, delaying tactics, and stalling tactics.
I find it very surprising that someone who is supposed to be an honourable Member questions the motives of Members across the way. He said that I do not speak up for western Canada, that I do not represent western Canada but rather union leaders in central Canada. That is nothing more or less than regional racism. It is regional racism of the worst kind. It is the kind of game which divides Canadians and is very divisive of the future unity of the country.
I do not question his western credentials. Of course he speaks up for western Canada. He has a different point of view than have I, but that does not make him less a westerner than am I. Why should I be less of a westerner or less of a Canadian than he is? That is the kind of nasty regional racism which divides the country. I am very surprised to hear someone from across the way with his experience say that kind of thing.
I voted against the Government in December, 1979, on a non-confidence motion because I thought the Budget was bad.
I did not defeat Joe Clark, the people of Canada defeated Joe Clark. A majority government was elected. The New Democratic Party caucus grew in size. The Conservatives lost western seats. In Saskatchewan, for example, the NDP went from five Members to seven and the Conservatives went from nine to seven. The people spoke.
That kind of arrogance and playing on divisiveness and racism turns people off of politicians. I just hope the Member across the way would not do that kind of thing. He says that because someone from western Canada speaks out against the trade deal, they are not a westerner. All he need do is look at the polls in western Canada. There are a lot of Manitobans, Albertans, people from Saskatchewan, and British Columbians who oppose this trade deal. In fact, until recently his Party
opposed this kind of a free trade deal with the United States. Year in and year out the Conservative Party led the crusade against such a trade deal with the United States.
Polls indicate that in Saskatchewan opinion is divided fifty-fifty, as the Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) knows. There was a rally in Regina recently, attended by a couple of thousand people who are opposed to this trade deal. There are all kinds of farmers in my riding who oppose this trade deal. They are concerned about the future of agriculture. That does not mean that they are not westerners or do not speak up for western Canada.
I just wish that we could have debates in this House in which we did not have to resort to this kind of divisiveness and name-calling but could talk about the issue on a substantive basis. That is what great leaders of the Conservative Party used to do. I think of the Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), a former Prime Minister, Mr. Stanfield, and others. Most people in that Party still debate issues on their substantive merits, but when we start using regional name-calling it degrades this place and creates an atmosphere in the country which is very disunifying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, maybe we are moving toward debates which centre on the issues. However, I sat here before I made my remarks and I did not hear much debate about the western diversification fund. I would like to leave the Member with a couple of pieces of information.
Deputy Minister-level meetings are occurring this very day between western diversification and Supply and Services to try to articulate the programs. Meetings at lower bureaucratic levels go on on a daily basis. They are trying to help western Canadian citizens access government programs and services in better ways than they used to. The Deputy Minister of Supply and Services and the Deputy Minister of Western Development met with all their provincial counterparts as recently as two weeks ago. This is the western way. Western Canada is composed of communities with pioneer roots. We have a volunteer tradition which all Canadians saw during the Olympics. We are used to working together.
I hope that the New Democratic Party would at least support this and we could use the extra 39 minutes to get this legislation into committee where it can be well vetted, returned for report stage and third reading, to become the law of the land in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, I am thrilled to rise to speak to Bill C-113, an Act to establish the western diversification office and subsequent offices in western Canada, and to lay out the framework to disburse funds in western Canada. This Bill represents an effort in terms of decentralization of decision-making and toward the diversification of the western economy. For those two reasons,
I certainly support the principle of this initiative.
March 2, 1988

I want to emphasize that the principles of this legislation are appropriate and honourable, ones that 1 and others have advocated for many years. There has been a need to diversify the economy of western Canada and move its dependency away from the resource industries, as valuable and important as they will always be, and to recognize the reality that the jobs of the future will move more toward these service sector industries, small scale manufacturing and a knowledge based economy.
While we ought to continue to develop the resources of western Canada as we have for many years, we should make greater efforts to finish more of those resources in western Canada and attempt to process these raw materials in western Canada. That is the challenge we face when it comes to developing our resources in western Canada so that we can move away from the extraction, development and growth of resources for overseas export which links us too closely to the vagaries of the international market. Our dependence on the resource sector gives us the traditional boom and bust economy of the West and ties us into the cyclical pricing of commodities on international markets. While that brings very good times, as we have seen recently, it also causes very tough times for westerners.
We certainly agree with the principles behind this Bill, but we have some real concerns about it as well. There is a feeling in western Canada that the federal Government has turned against westerners to a certain extent. While I am not sure people feel betrayed, they are certainly surprised that more has not happened in western Canada considering the overwhelming number of westerners in the Cabinet, from the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) to a number of other senior cabinet Ministers. It seems that there has not been the resurgence and support of the western economy that people had expected.
I need go no further than my constituency and surrounding constituencies in western Canada, including the Caribou constituencies, northern B.C. constituencies, the Kootenays and Okanagan Valley constituencies.
I do not believe that many people in those constituencies would agree that their lives have been better or more secure than they were in 1984 when this Government was elected. In fact, those to whom I have spoken have indicated that they do not have the same feeling of confidence for the future, particularly for their children and grandchildren.
For example, one can consider the re-emergence of the Western Canada Concept and the Confederation of Regions Party. These parties are gaining strength in western Canada, primarily from the right of the political spectrum, which normally include disillusioned Conservatives who believe that the West has not benefited as much as it should have, considering the overwhelming number of western Conservatives in the Government.
Western Economic Diversification Act
What is the reason for this disillusionment? Let us consider Bill C-113. It provides $1.2 billion over five years for all of western Canada, comprising four provinces. Goodness knows that the Liberals certainly abandoned any support for the West when they were in power, but they introduced the Western Development Fund of $4 billion over four years. The Conservatives are introducing a significantly smaller amount of money through this program we are debating, which seems to suggest that compared to the Liberals, matters seems to be worse in terms of western Canada.
We can study this further by examining federal Government sourcing through agencies, which has a tremendous impact on the regional economy. If federal Government Crown corporations like Petro-Canada, Air Canada, CNR and others were to purchase much of their goods and services from western Canadian suppliers, it would give a real boost to the economy in western Canada. Elowever, let me quote from Supply and Services statistics. In 1981 western Canada received about 15 per cent of all the money invested in supply and services by the federal Government. In 1984, that decreased to 14 per cent, and by 1987 had decreased to 11 per cent. In other words, the amount of sourcing from western Canada relative to the rest of Canada is less than it had been when the federal Government took office. One can only assume that the Supply and Services figures are accurate.
Let us consider the Industrial Regional Development Program and the value of contracts given across Canada, noting the population in western Canada. Once again, we received less than our fair share based on the population of western Canada relative to central Canada.
If one wanted to make a case for an affirmative economic program for western Canada, perhaps one could even argue that western Canada should get even more than it deserves considering the high levels of unemployment in western Canada compared to central Canada. Presumably this is another indication of why people are disenchanted with what is happening in terms of economic development in western Canada.
Let us consider regional development programs which are primarily meant to assist regions like those in western Canada. In 1984, the federal Government was spending $14.8 billion on regional development programs. As our Estimates would indicate, in 1987 regional development programs amounted to only $11.8 billion. In other words, $3 billion over a three-year period was plucked out of regional development programs which, by and large, go into helping areas like western Canada. I am wearing a button today which says: "Go with the flow". This button represents our concern regarding the Government's decision to cut back on flow-through shares to assist the mining industry. We all know that the flow-through share program provided a tremendous incentive, encouragement and nurturing of the exploration programs that eventually led to mining property development and, hopefully, mines.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Everywhere in Canada from the western Arctic, to British Columbia, up to the Yukon, right across northern Canada to Labrador, a tremendous amount of mineral exploration is taking place because of this particular initiative, the flowthrough share program. The Government's response to this is to essentially gut the flow-through share program. This is the kind of thing that makes us wonder how committed the Government is to western economic development programs.
I do not have to remind Members of the maintenance contract for the CF-18. Virtually every single adviser suggested that the maintenance program should go to the West. However, the Government decided it should not go to the West. If we are going to make decisions based on politics, let us be up front about it. We were going to make the decision based on economics or the professional advice we received, but when 75 advisers out of 75 said the contract should go to the West, the Government ignored that advice. As a westerner, I can only assume that the Government's priorities appear not to be the development and support of the economy of western Canada.
I can also talk about the CN cuts. I notice the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is in the House of Commons. He will know that over the last number of years, unfortunately, we have seen a number of positions cut in CN. Because the lion's share of rail activity takes place in the transportation infrastructure of western Canada, once again it is western Canada that is essentially the hardest hit in terms of those cut-backs initiated throughout the rail system.
There is also Challenge '88. That is the program where the Government helps to fund college, vocational, technical and university students for the summer. We all recognize that inflation year after year requires that these programs be increased marginally to keep up with the rate of inflation. However, during the past two years the allotments of the federal Government for the summer work program for students have not increased at all, which means, when one factors in inflation, that there have actually been serious cuts to the amount of money the federal Government provides for summer jobs. Of course, the problem is most acute in western and eastern Canada. In pockets of central Canada we have a tremendous amount of economic prosperity and the chances for a summer job are much greater than in areas of western Canada where unemployment rates are now in the 20 per cent to 30 per cent range, which makes it very difficult, if not impossible, for young people to find employment.
I do not think anyone would question the fact that if we are going to have economic prosperity in western Canada, we have to invest more in the most important natural resource of western Canada. When I refer to the most important natural resource, I do not mean wheat, timber, coal, gas, oil or minerals. 1 mean people. When we invest in developing the most important natural resource in western Canada, the people, it means we have to spend more money on education
and training programs. However, when we look at the amount of money allocated for training over the last number of years, we find the Government has not increased but has cut funding for those programs.
Last year, the Estimates indicate that $479 million existed for employment programs. This year it will be $339 million. That is a $140 million cut in the amount of money going for training and education. All of us who have universities and colleges in our areas realize that Employment Canada has been forced to cut the number of seats it normally would fund to assist people to train and upgrade and improve their skills. In that critical area, the development of human resources, there seems to be cut-backs.
I suppose what has most obviously affected western Canada has been the decision of the Government to cut back in funding for the Post Office. It requires that the Post Office make money. It is one government service the Government decided should make profits. We do not expect the military to make profits. We do not expect the RCMP, ambulance services, universities and colleges or hospitals to make profits. We do not expect the Department of Immigration to make a profit. However, we do expect the Post Office to make a profit, that one government service that touches the lives of every single Canadian in every Canadian community for their entire life. In a country as vast as Canada, where we are trying to service rural areas and small communities, we have to cut back on the amount of service we provide.
Where do we cut back if we are trying to make an efficient profit-making organization of the Post Office? We do not cut back in Montreal or Toronto. We cut back in the rural areas, the post offices in the small communities. Where do they exist? They exist in western Canada. That is the part of Canada where rural areas and small communities are being depopulated at an ever accelerating rate. There seems to be a lack of commitment by the Government in terms of maintaining a dignified rural life in western Canada because we are seeing the erosion of government services, the most obvious being postal services.
What we see in this legislation is a bit of an illusion. It gives the impression that the Government is interested in the economy of western Canada and the diversification of the economy of western Canada, but I think if it really was it would not have excluded, for example, the ability of communities to redevelop their urban structures and to expand their community development.
For some mysterious reason the Government has decided that the western diversification fund will not be used for urban or community development. In other words, it will not be used to improve sewage treatment or water systems, to build roads or to provide community facilities. If we are going to diversify the economy of western Canada, it is imperative that those communities be vibrant communities. If we are going to encourage the development of service industries, high-tech industries and modern manufacturing, we must have good
March 2, 1988

universities, colleges, technical schools and vocational schools. If the basic urban infrastructure is not there, it is going to be more difficult than ever to expand those particular facilities.
I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that every provincial Government across Canada, barring none, has said they are prepared to participate in a municipal infrastructure sharing program. They say they will pay one-third, the local taxpayers in the area will pay one-third and the federal Government kicks in one-third. In other words, there will be a one-third cost sharing program to develop urban infrastructure. The provinces, cities and municipalities across Canada unanimously agreed. Only one person did not. That was the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). He said he was not interested in participating in the development of rural infrastructures using this method.
1 could go on and talk about the need to expand Government procurement and the need for programs to encourage the development of our tourist industry, small business and manufacturing in western Canada, and programs to assist in the development of value added for our resource industries, but I think what is needed more than ever is a development strategy. The western diversification fund is really a grab bag. For example, British Columbia, $79 million over five years will be used for South Moresby Park. That money should have more rightfully come from the social policy reserve fund or the Parks Canada fund, not from the western diversification fund. The $53 million in British Columbia to be spent over five years for salmon enhancement should come from the Department of Fisheries, not from the western diversification fund.
There was the $10 million bail out for the Fraser Valley Shakes and Shingles Association after the devastating decision by the Government regarding shakes and shingles exports. We are already seeing a major part of the fund eaten up with programs that should be rightfully funded from other government departments. We do not have a comprehensive strategy in terms of developing proper facilities for our urban communities.
We have not developed proper over-all strategies in terms of western transportation and communication, the development of our river systems and soil preservation policies in the West. What is the strategy, what is the business or economic blueprint we are trying to introduce into western Canada? As I see it at the moment, it seems to be simply a grab bag. Whatever one can convince the decision makers of will be funded or there will be a grant or loan guarantee or whatever.
O)
In closing, I say that we agree in principle that this type of approach is necessary. However, in terms of a real commitment that is honest and real to diversify the economy of western Canada, it does not seem to be here in this particular legislation.
Western Economic Diversification Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg).

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and a question. I listened with interest to the discourse of my hon. colleague from British Columbia. I must admit that I was somewhat confused when he asked the rhetorical question that he said he asked his constituents. The question was, "Are you better off now in 1988 than you were in 1984?" He told us that his constituents responded in the negative. When I ask that question in my riding, the response is positive.
My constituents acknowledge that the federal Government has spent more in reforestation money than any other federal Government. They state that housing starts are at a new high in Canada. They state that it is now cheaper to borrow money than it ever was before. They remind me that the unemployment rate on central Vancouver Island was 17 per cent when I was elected and that it is now some 10 per cent. This means that 90 per cent of my constituents are working.
It seems to me that the people of Nanaimo-Alberni see the glass as being half full while NDP riding associations and NDP Members see it as being half empty. This probably comes from having a pro-active Member of Parliament, a positive Member of Parliament, as opposed to having a reactive and negative Member of Parliament.
The Hon. Member attacked the Government's position on flow-through shares. He stated that he is wearing a button which states, "Go with the flow". I cannot understand how the NDP can justify attacking big business and big corporations for not paying enough tax and yet support just such a tax measure which would employ people. They cannot have it both ways. Can my colleague respond to that?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the chance to respond to my hon. friend. With respect to the flow-through share issue it benefits primarily companies that are not in a profit situation. That is the idea of a flow through. The flow through goes to an investor beyond the actual exploration company involved.
I am pleased to say that the flow-through share program benefits not quite exclusively but largely Canadian junior companies, Canadian owned companies. It is a good program. It has generated a tremendous amount of mining activity across Canada. That is why I think it should be preserved. That is why perhaps even tomorrow, which is an opposition day, we might take some initiative to ensure that the debate on the flow-through share issue is continued.
With respect to my friend's original comment, perhaps it would be useful for him to discuss the situation with his Kootenay colleagues. Two of his friends, Conservative Members of Parliament, represent Kootenay ridings where the unemployment rate is now about 20 per cent. My recollection is that back in 1984 it was also about 20 per cent. For that part of British Columbia things have not changed significantly.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
I suggest that he also spend some time with his Conservative colleague from the Cariboo region of British Columbia. In that region the unemployment rates have not changed substantially since 1984.
To say that every initiative that the Government has taken is bad would be inappropriate. There is more funding going into reforestation in British Columbia than there was under the Liberals by some margin. However, I like to think that if we were serious about regional economic development, and I suspect that my hon. friend will agree, that while there have been more advances and more efforts made in terms of husbanding our forest resource much more could be done.
I want to share with the Hon. Member what took place at a meeting I had recently with a number of professional foresters in my constituency. They were asked how many men and women could actually be employed to develop the forest resource as it ought to be developed in central British Columbia, particularly in the Kamloops reforestation district. They said in terms of thinning, spacing, fertilizing, disease control, pest control, road building and a whole variety of other programs that as many as 10,000 men and women could be employed over a vast number of years. That is what we should be doing if we are going to develop our resource, as is done in places such as Finland, for example. I suspect that the Hon. Member would agree that that would be an appropriate initiative to take.
Rather than providing funds for unemployment insurance or indirectly through welfare, why not develop programs with our forest companies, in co-operation with our provincial Governments, to develop and to husband that critical forest resource, not only in western Canada but right across Canada? This would put literally tens of thousands of Canadians to work at something that must be done. It would not be a make work program. It is something that must be done in order to develop a critical Canadian resource.

Mr. Speaker, in sitting here this afternoon listening to the debate I am having a little difficulty with it because I am a new Member of the House. I have only been here since 1984. I can only reflect on how things were then and how things are now in my own riding.
My background is in small business. I am a farmer. People who have sat here for the length of time that some of the Members in the New Democratic Party have sat here have been out of touch with reality for a little too long. They review how things were then and how they are now.
The fact is that interest rates have made a fantastic difference to agriculture and to small business. Just look at the unemployment rate and the way it is now. I lived through those years. 1 was in business and in agriculture. It was very difficult to survive in those years, thanks to the way things were. Interest rates were at an all-time high. I do not have to tell anyone who is in small business or in agriculture about this. They have only to look back at their records for 1981 and
1982 to see that they were paying interest rates of 22.5 per cent and 22.75 per cent and higher. I have but to remind them who was in government then. It was the Liberals who were in power as a result of the New Democratic Party defeating the Conservative Government.
We have brought in legislation. It was first announced on August 4, 1987, by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). This legislation is to promote diversification of the economy in western Canada.
I would like to share with the Hon. Member something that I read in the Moose Jaw paper. It is from the January 30, 1988, edition. The article states that a Moose Jaw company has gone high tech thanks to assistance from the western diversification fund. Is this fund not working? What would the Hon. Member call that then? Other firms in Moose Jaw are also receiving assistance from the western diversification initiative.
Why do we not pass this legislation? What is the big debate about? Do Members of the New Democratic Party intend to stand here speaker after speaker and lament their past and all the sins they have committed in the past with the Liberals? Let us bring this matter to a vote.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that no one here would say that the $1.2 billion as spread out over five years will not do any good for anybody. No one is saying that. I think that is what the Hon. Member is implying.
In response to the Hon. Member's point that some people are out of touch with reality, I would point out to him that there was an NDP nomination meeting in his constituency on February 20. In 1984 there were 200 people at the NDP nomination meeting.
In 1984 there were 1,500 people at the PC nomination meeting.

On February 20 there were 700 people at the nomination meeting. The number went from 200 to 700. I think there is a new wind blowing down there in Moose Jaw. If the Hon. Member wants to do the right thing, he should probably spend a lot more time back home rather than standing here in the House of Commons making nonsensical comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-113. It has been interesting to listen to Hon. Members across the way participate in the debate. They are telling us how great it is today with the Tories in power and with all the initiatives that are being taken under the Western Economic Diversification Program. Clearly, it would be desirable to see how much the program will do for western Canada.
It is easy to see how the Government is able to gussy up the $220 million per year to run the program if we simply look at


March 2, 1988

the tremendous cut-backs that have been made over the last three and a half years by the federal Government. If one looks at that, combined with the massive increase in personal taxation, it is not difficult to see where the Government will come up with the extra money to fund this program which, let's face it, is a very modest program. It is interesting to note that all of those programs are calculated over a five-year period.
During 1983-84 the previous Liberal Government committed some $1.2 billion to western Canada in a two-year period under the ERDA program. That amount was increased to $2.1 billion because it provided for matching funds from the provinces. The amount of money that we are looking at is not very great when one considers the type of cut-backs that have taken place.
A few days ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) announced approximately $25 million worth of branch line rehabilitation projects. Of course, they came out with a nice blue label giving the Minister's name on each sheet and stating that they were jointly announced by people like the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Gustafson), wherein he announced that he was going to carry out the rehabilitation of a line in his constituency amounting to several hundred thousand dollars. In fact, there was one for $165,000.
What the Minister of Transport did not announce in this program is that, by the end of the period, 1990, when the more than $1 billion program will be complete, $125 million will be left in the program unspent. A program that is desperately needed for rehabilitation and upgrading of the rail lines throughout western Canada in order to move grain and wheat to market will have money left unspent and will lapse. I assume that it will never be used.
For instance, the Wood Mountain subdivision was supposed to be rehabilitated. In these announcements, 1 do not see any indication that that subdivision will be rehabilitated. 1 understand that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, the person who wears the flak jacket and harangues the troops and tells them about how bad the NDP defence policy is, has had many representations. He has attended meetings. Still, the money will not come.
It is clear that the Minister of Transport is siphoning off approximately $125 million from the rail line rehabilitation program in western Canada that was supposed to be spent on rehabilitating those rail lines in order that crops could be moved to market more rapidly. I suppose it is being shifted over into the department of western economic diversification. In fact, it is a type of shell game. There is $1 billion here, but we are not going to spend $125 million of that, so we will create another department over here. In fact, approximately one-third of the funding for the first year will likely come out of that fund.
An Hon. Member asked how things were three or four years ago, and how they are now. Three or four years ago the price of grain in western Canada was $170 a tonne for No. 1 wheat.
Western Economic Diversification Act
A few years prior to that time, it was close to $200. This year it is $110. Barley and oats are much lower than that.
How far does a $220 million per year program go in covering that type of reduction in income for grain farmers? In fact, it is totally irrelevant. The devastation which has been wreaked on western communities, entire community life, and the stress on individuals, has not been seen since R. B. Bennett was in power during those terrible years from 1930 to 1935.
How have the Tories responded to this situation? If we look at the debt situation, the signals were clear and unmistakable in the fall of 1984 when the Farm Credit Corporation signalled that we were facing one of the worst farm debt crises since the 1930s. Very little, if anything, with regard to the farm debt crisis happened for the first year or so.
In the spring of 1985 the Minister finally got around to bringing in the farm debt review boards. Those boards do not have any power to reschedule debt or refinance farmers' loans. They are very modest programs. Some people suggest that all they do is silence everybody in sight, from the people on the board to the farmer, to the advisers, to the local pool operators, to everybody involved.
When the Government finally moved on some debt restructuring programs, it brought in the commodity based mortgage which was designed to help a couple of thousand farmers per year for the last two or three years.
We are faced with the situation in Saskatchewan and other parts of the Prairies where there are some 50,000 farmers in serious financial difficulty, some 12,000 of whom are totally insolvent. The Farm Credit Corporation started appealing a year ago last fall for funds to revitalize a recovery program for the Farm Credit Corporation. No action has yet been taken.
The Minister surreptitiously filed the Farm Credit Corporation's report on the last day the House sat last June. It showed that the Farm Credit Corporation was insolvent to the tune of $124 million. It is expected that that will be more than $300 million for the current fiscal year. How can this corporation help farmers in serious financial difficulty to reschedule debt, set aside debt, or overcome these difficulties when it is insolvent?
The magnitude and the gravity of the situation in western Canada has gone down every year since, and no effective action has been taken with regard to the farm debt crisis. I guess the double whammy of the whole situation is the Western Accord which the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources negotiated with the prairie Tory Premiers. It was hailed as a great step forward. Everybody believed that until the spring of 1986 when the world price of oil collapsed. The price dropped from $28 a barrel to $10, recovering to $18 a barrel last summer. Oil is now around $16 a barrel. If it was so good, why did this great negotiation not take into account the precipitous drops in the price of oil that we have seen, as well as the recession and depression that fell on Alberta and Saskatchewan during that period?

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
It is common for the Tories to talk about how tough things were in the recession years of 1981-82. But they were not nearly as bad as in the summer of 1986 and early 1987 and which is continuing, when oil prices were at the $15 or $16 a barrel level. The situation has been made worse with the appreciation of the Canadian dollar, creating the double whammy. The cut-backs and the pounding down of western community life continues. Its very vitality is being removed, and I do not see how a couple of hundred million dollars, or $220 million a year, can really diversify the entire western economy.
In northern Ontario, Atlantic Canada and other resource areas the Government has hit us with several double whammies in support for community colleges. There has been a cutback in funding by 40 per cent. The number of seats in community colleges has been reduced by 40 per cent right across the country. The oil industry in Alberta and the grain industry right across the Prairies has been suffering hardship. When people want to retrain, the seats are not available because of the 40 per cent cut-back.
Likewise, the Government is hell-bent on a program in rural Canada to remove and privatize post offices, replacing home delivery with superboxes. Many communities already feeling the pinch and suffering from a reduction in population are having their post office removed, resulting in one less job. Across the country 9,200 jobs will be lost, 80 per cent of which are held by women. Over 5,000 post offices will be affected.
Interestingly enough, the resource areas have benefited tremendously from the earned depletion allowance for the mineral industry. Signals went out last spring that it was to be cut. Yesterday at the Renaissance Hotel in Ottawa there was a conference to encourage the protesting of the Government's decision to cut out the earned depletion allowance. This has been providing some $400 million to $500 million for mining exploration and development, especially in western Canada, northern Ontario, northern Quebec and other resource areas.
The program should be reinstated. It has been providing $400 million to $500 million. That money is important because it creates activity in diamond drilling, exploration and development. Diversifying the economy in a mineral area is extremely difficult. The flow-through share mechanism with an earned depletion allowance of 33 per cent is extremely difficult to replace with any other mechanism. Not only are exploration and development dollars spent by diamond drilling teams and so on, but mines are established.
A number of mines in northern Ontario are being brought into production because of the earned depletion allowance provided by the Government. Clearly, every Member in the government caucus, including Members from Timmins, Abitibi, Quebec and Timiskaming in Ontario who have spoken out, will have a chance on Monday evening-the motion will be put on Friday-to vote for or against the replacement of the
earned depletion allowance which affects not only northern Canada but western Canada as well.
Another action taken by the Government relates to the decision on the softwood lumber deal with the United States. The full effect of this deal, which is costing the resource producing areas of Canada, including British Columbia, some $500 million a year will not be felt until the downturn occurs both in the Canadian market and in the United States.
I read a report a couple of weeks ago by a lumber company in Prince George, British Columbia. Under the previous arrangement, the company was paying $600 million a year in stumpage charges. But under the deal negotiated with the B.C. Government, the federal Government and the United States, this company will now be paying $19 million a year in stumpage charges. The company said that when the market turns down it will be out of business.
There is a concerted attack on rural resource areas and in all areas of activity in the West. Whether we see a dramatic downturn in grain prices, the farm debt crisis or the deal negotiated on oil, clearly all these attacks on the western economy will not be overcome by a program which provides a couple of hundred million dollars a year in a diversification fund.
There is a diversification program in northern Ontario. Although it was signalled in the fall of 1986 and announced last summer, there are no application forms or criteria yet available. I understand much the same situation exists in western Canada. A program is announced, money is announced but the actual criteria for projects are not available. The actual application forms are not available. The implementation is simply not there. Rural infrastructure which is desperately needed by many rural communities is excluded from the program. We have to ask ourselves, in the face of the tremendous onslaught that has taken place, is it really too little too late to help western Canada with all the problems it faces in economic development and diversification?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment on the some of the statements that were made about western Canada. The debate that has been going on boils down to assessing what has and has not been done by various Governments. Certainly the Hon. Member who just spoke, who himself was a part of the National Energy Program committee, knows what that devastating legislation put in by the Liberal Government did to western Canada.
Let us look at the record of our Government over the past three years. The farmers of western Canada and particularly those of the area I represent have never been treated better in difficult times. We went through a drought and difficult prices in the international market-place. Just yesterday, the farmers of western Canada received the first payment on the grains payment.
March 2, 1988

Comparing what the Liberal administration did in western Canada during good times and what our Government has done in a short term, 1 can tell Hon. Members that the farmers in general are very supportive of this Government. There will be people from the other two Parties who will vote for our Government in the next election based on the performance of this Government.
The Hon. Member mentioned the rail lines. I would like to make a statement about the rail lines in my riding. I am very pleased that the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is in the House to hear this. A great deal of the credit goes to him for what has been accomplished.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) attended the meeting in Minton a week ago Saturday when we went to bat for the problem that exists there, and I thank him for his help. I especially want to thank the Minister for the quick action he took on including money to be spent on rail line improvements for the completion of the Bromhead-Minton line and the Fife Lake line.
1 do not know where the Hon. Member is getting his information from. I am the first to admit that there is still more work to be done. We do want to see the completion of the Bengough line, and I am sure we will. The Hon. Member is trying to leave the impression that action has not been taken in western Canada on the rail lines and on the welfare of farmers. That absolutely misrepresents the situation and I just wanted to clarify that.

Mr. Speaker, it was very interesting to listen to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister and to note the apple polishing he is doing for the benefit of the Minister of Transport. I assume he is doing that because he is having difficulty getting the Minister to do improvements on the Wood Mountain subdivision of the railway. Clearly it does not appear that any decision has been made on that by the Minister. 1 suppose that would explain why the Hon. Member is doing so much apple polishing.
1 think it is up to the Parliamentary Secretary, who obviously has tremendous clout in the Tory caucus, to put the hammer down on the Minister of Transport so that he does not leave $125 million in the rail line rehabilitation program pot. That is exactly what is going on. I do not know how the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary will be able to say to the people of these various communities: "Well, we tried, but the Minister had already nixed the balance of the program".
In the way the program has been delivered, there does not seem to be any money for the Wood Mountain subdivision. The Parliamentary Secretary attended the meeting and promised that there would be action. He went to the Minister but got no action. The only alternative he has is to go directly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
I know the Parliamentary Secretary has the ear of the Prime Minister. He is briefed with the Prime Minister every morning on all the national issues of the day. I would hope that he
Western Economic Diversification Act
would put pressure on the Prime Minister to get the Minister of Transport to ensure that the other rail lines get completed.
I wonder how the Parliamentary Secretary could be so happy about telling us that he has done all these wonderful things for agriculture while there is still a very large number of farmers facing total insolvency and serious financial difficulties. The Government brought in a very minor program, the commodity-based mortgage program, which provides for about 2,000 mortgages at around 8 per cent across the entire country over two years.
The magnitude of the problem we face today is unprecedented since the 1930s. There are 50,000 farmers in serious financial difficulty. The Government brought in a program a couple of years ago that provides benefits for a couple of thousand farmers. These benefits are only available to people who have mortgages under the Farm Credit Corporation. If a farmer has a mortgage with the Royal Bank or the Bank of Commerce and is hard pressed, the program does not apply.
Surely, if the Parliamentary Secretary were really doing his job with the Prime Minister and with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), he would get that program expanded so that it would cover a good percentage of farmers. There are 16,000 farmers with FCC loans, not to mention all the other mortgages that are outstanding, who are two years in arrears with their mortgages.
The Parliamentary Secretary has been telling us what great things have been done, but he has not explained everything. Perhaps we just assume that the way it will be is that oil prices will be $16 a barrel instead of $28 a barrel when the Tories are in power. Tory times are hard times so we have to be ready for them. Instead of being $200 a tonne, grain prices are $110 a tonne. It is a given that times will be tough and that the Tories will then have to do something about it.
I do not think that a modest program like this one, which provides a couple of hundred million dollars per year for economic diversification in western Canada, will be adequate to cover all of the tremendous economic downturns with which western Canada is faced, let alone the irresponsible cut-backs that have taken place to community college funding, the earned depletion allowance, the post office and every aspect of community life. I am depending on the Parliamentary Secretary to beef up this program and to make it a little more responsible and effective so that it will really help western Canada in its hour of need.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to hear the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) say that we should beef up the program. I certainly support that as well.
The Government is spending only $1.2 billion over five years, $60 million per province per year. That is not very much money. The Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) would agree that we must be very disappointed that the Government is only spending $1.2 billion.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
Five or six years ago, the Liberals had a western development fund with some $4 billion. The Tories across the way were criticizing it as being too small. The Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) was saying how stingy the Liberal Government was to provide funds for western Canada of only $4 billion. That was not even spent.
1 just wanted to comment that I think the Hon. Member for Algoma was right when he said $1.2 billion is appreciated, but it is not very much. It is only $60 million for Saskatchewan every year. By the way, most of that money was already there anyway in different government programs, and it is now being funnelled into this program. It is a nice little program for Tory re-election prospects even though there has never been a Government in Canada as unpopular as that Government. Recent polls tell us that the Government is even more unpopular than the Trudeau Government, which is absolutely incredible.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated that explanation. I saw the same poll which indicated 52 per cent thought it did a better job than the present Government, which got only 23 per cent support. I want to leave lots of time for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister to defend his boss. He can explain how the Government of former Prime Minister Trudeau is seen by people as doing a better job than his own Government.
I think 1 saw the height of apology for the Government last year when the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) took total responsibility for the Government not putting up a loan guarantee for the Syncrude project. I know the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister and a number of others of us went to an excellent briefing on why the federal Government should come up with its share of the loan guarantee. The guarantee would only come into effect if the price of oil went below some $15 a barrel. 1 do not think it has ever gone below that price since the fall of 1986.
The Prime Minister promised action but he did not take action. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said he had not explained well enough to the Minister why the loan guarantee was needed. Everyone in the Alberta caucus, including the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), realized how important it was to increase the capacity of the Syncrude plant. The program went ahead under a loan guarantee from Alberta, but you kind of wonder why the Parliamentary Secretary has to take the rap for not explaining how important the project was.
I just do not see how $60 million a year in loan guarantees and grants and contributions for each province is going to be adequate to overcome the support which should have been forthcoming directly from the Government and not cobbled up into this program we are debating today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with
great interest to the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) and the Hon. Member from the NDP. Anyone watching that debate will clearly understand the coalition between the NDP and the Liberal Party.
I must respond first to the remarks by the Hon. Member for Algoma concerning the Syncrude capacity addition project presented to the Government of Canada in which the Syncrude consortium asked for a loan guarantee. I would like to enlighten the Hon. Member that it was not the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who refused the loan guarantee. It was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his Department. The reason they gave was that the project would go ahead without it. They do not need a loan guarantee. All it is, is show. We could very well do it but if we did, it would add to the federal deficit and take money away from another area necessary to meeting our deficit goal.
At the time 1 was disappointed that we did not go ahead with the political show of a loan guarantee to that project, but in retrospect the Minister of Finance was correct in every detail. The project did go ahead without the loan guarantee. It was a wise decision on his part.
I cannot imagine being a member of the Liberal Party standing up and speaking against the western diversification program. 1 cannot fathom how this could happen from Members of Parliament who sat in this House and voted in favour of a National Energy Program which totally and absolutely devastated western Canada. That Member stood in his place and spoke in favour of the NEP which totally devastated the communities where I and everyone else in western Canada live.
I want to tell him what was happening there, admitted to by the former Liberal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Marc Lalonde. He now stands up in Montreal and says the reason they brought in the NEP was because they wanted to divert money from the western provinces into the coffers of the central Government. That is what the Hon. Member stood for and that is what the NDP stood for. They were on their feet supporting the NEP. Their energy critic stood in this House and said the program does not go far enough. What we should be doing is nationalizing one of the big ones. Nationalize Imperial Oil is what they were saying. It amounted to total devastation of western Canada. This Government is now trying to repair some of the damage that those two Parties sitting in coalition did to western Canada.
Then they have the gall to stand up in this House and say we are not going far enough to support western diversification.

Point of order, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if the Hon. Member could explain why PetroCan bought out Gulf Oil, spending about $1 billion of taxpayers' money? When the Tories came to power they bought out Gulf Oil-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to answer that question after my remarks. The Hon. Member is getting a little hot in his seat. He understands where I am coming from and that what I am saying is true. It really bothers the hon. gentleman when the facts are laid down in front of him.
The NEP put thousands of companies in Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan out of business. It put thousands of people out of work. It totally dried up the industry. Do you remember the Alsands project which was ready to go north of Fort McMurray? It was going to create something like 4,000 jobs and add another 10 per cent to the oil supply. I remember that one. I saw what the NEP did to the community of Fort McMurray. I saw what it did to Edmonton and Calgary. I saw what it did to all those drilling and exploration companies. 1 saw what it did, and for a Member who was part of the Liberal Government at that time and members of the NDP to stand up and speak against a program we are putting in place to help diversify the economy of western Canada is totally and absolutely immoral. They know full well that they were supporting the devastation of western Canada because they had a pie-in-the-sky idea. They said that they were going to have a made-in-Canada price for oil. They attempted to rob from western Canada and put it in the central Canada coffers.
How much will the $220 million a year that is going into western Canada do for western Canada? It is obvious that we have the problems which we do with regard to the deficit because all the former Government did was throw money. It did not use money in a sensible way as an incentive to bring on industry, development, and diversification. It threw money down the tube.
People remember what the Scientific Research Tax Credit did. There was such a big hole in that legislation that you could drive a Mack truck loaded with manure through it. That truck was driven through it and it cost and is still costing the Treasury of the federal Government billions of dollars. That is the kind of fiscal responsibility we saw from the Liberal Government which was supported, in many instances, by the NDP which now talks about coalition.
We heard that today in the debate. I could not tell who was speaking only by listening. I heard the same garbage from the Liberals as I heard from the NDP and I heard the same garbage from the NDP as I heard from the Liberals. They have already decided that they will form a coalition. They have looked at the polls and have decided that the Conservative Party would form a minority government if an election was held today, and they would therefore form a coalition. They have admitted that and talked about it.
Let us look at the NDP record. Let us look at what the NDP has done since we came to office. The NDP voted against the Patent Act and against removal of the National Energy Policy. Members of the NDP voted against the Western Accord which we drew up with western Canada and against the Atlantic
Western Economic Diversification Act
Accord. They want nothing but central control on industry and development. You never hear the NDP talking about diversifying the automotive industry out of Oshawa because they have Bob White and Shirley Carr to contend with. I do not know if it really matters to the New Democratic Party Leader. I do not know where he takes his orders. I think they pull a lever in Shirley Carr's office and the toilet flushes in the office of the Leader of the NDP.
The transportation Bill removed for all time discrimination in western Canada in rail transportation and the NDP voted against it. NDP Members spent six days debating the Senate amendments to the Immigration Act while we have a very real problem with immigration with which we are struggling daily. However, we had better not put that law in place because they would not be able to stand up in the House of Commons and go after the Minister of Immigration because some guy lied his way into Canada and we cannot deport him without going through a number of processes.
We spent nine days debating the Budget. Do you remember when we were trying to put the postal workers back to work, Mr. Speaker? Where did the members of the NDP stand on that? They stood up and voted not to put them back to work. We must have postal service in western Canada. We are not prepared to use courier services as they can in Toronto, Oshawa, and Montreal. We must have mail service in every community in the country, particularly in western Canada where we rely upon it so much.
We introduced legislation to put the grain handlers back to work. If you do not move the grain in western Canada, the farmers are out in the cold. The NDP voted against that as well.
It was very interesting to hear the debate today and see how much the two Parties meld together with a total lack of understanding of the problems in western Canada. The western diversification program is an historic move in this country. For once we have a western diversification program and a Minister responsible for western diversification who is from the West. We have an office and a Deputy Minister located in Edmonton where they can deal with the problems facing the West. That move alone diversifies some of the government bureaucracy with which we are faced.
Let us talk about the farmers. I heard the Member for Algoma stand up and plead the plight of the farmer. I heard the NDP stand up and plead the plight of the farmer. The present Government is the first Government that has reacted and done what has to be done for the farmers in western Canada. The Liberal Government brought in a 25-cent tax on gasoline which the farmers had to pay. We removed that in order that input costs would go down.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker. Do you remember the Canadian ownership charge at the pumps? An oil company created under the National Energy Program had its hand in every pocket in this country.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
We do not for a moment say that the farming industry does not have problems. Certainly it does. However, even with a grain war waging between the United States and the European Common Market, we moved more grain this year than in any other year. We have given more help to the farmers across the country than has any other government in living memory. We have given $5 billion in assistance since we came to office. We will continue to assist the farming community in that way because we came to office with a commitment to the farm community and we have lived up to that commitment.
What is the western diversification program about? It was introduced by the western diversification office and is part of a mandate to manage the western diversification fund which was set up to stimulate diversification in the country, particularly in western Canada. It is designed in such a way as to give maximum flexibility in dealing with proposals which may come forward for western diversification fund assistance.
We always had programs designed in Ottawa in the ivory towers which we then had to make work. We were given the guidelines, the rules, and the regulations. That did not work. I can remember the old tier system and the process which had to be gone through to change it. It was based on census and employment figures. We had great disparity in the country.
There were tier 1 areas, some tier 2 areas and others that were tier 3. All of Alberta was not even considered. Alberta had gone through a period of relative prosperity until the Liberals and NDP decided to devastate Canada with their national energy policy. That threw a monkey-wrench into the whole system.
Even when there were 40,000 unemployed in Edmonton alone we did not have a chance with the tier system because it took too long to deal with our situation. In Calgary, houses and apartments were empty, businesses were going down the tube and people were being thrown out of work day after day. Yet the formula did not allow us to benefit from the economic development system.
We now have a program that has the required flexibility because the criteria has been designed in an office in Edmonton, in consultation with the people whom it will affect. The program is geared to support projects that promote or enhance economic development or diversify in some way western Canada. It includes the initiation, the promotion or expansion of enterprises, the establishment of new business, research and development activities. However, these activities will be controlled. We will not bring in a scientific research tax credit system whereby scams can take billions of dollars out of the Treasury without anything being done.
It has been suggested that this program is a smoke and mirrors exercise to make us look good. This is a flexible program that responds to the needs of western Canada. It will not have a tier structure. The West will be treated as a single region.
We will all be in tears.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The Member says that they will all be in tears. I wonder where his tears will be when people begin to realize how lock-step the NDP and Liberals really are in the House of Commons. I would ask anyone reading today's Hansard to block out the names of those speaking on this Bill and identify whether they are NDP or Liberals. They would certainly be able to identify the Conservative Members, but the Liberals and New Democrats are lock-step with one another. They have already formed the coalition about which they have been talking.
The eligible costs have been broadened to include working capital because we found that the need for working capital sometimes created a problem. Previous programs had always been geared more to the wealthy who had the working capital and good solid backing. Now we have broadened the eligible costs through the western diversification program to include working capital. Many small businesses would like to expand but need the financing for capital expansion as well as working capital, which anyone in business will suggest is the hardest financing to obtain.
If I sitting in the Liberal or NDP benches, particularly considering the history I saw here between 1980 and 1984, I would be ashamed to stand up against the western diversification office and the western diversification program.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) claims that his Party does very well in representing western Canada. The statistics I have from Statistics Canada show that of the goods and services purchased by the Department of Supply and Services in 1981-82,
15.5	per cent was purchased in the West. In 1984-85, the first year that his Party took power, goods and services purchased in the West went down to 13.9 per cent and dropped to some
11.5	per cent in 1986-87.
Why is the federal Government purchasing less in western Canada? A decrease from 13.9 per cent to 11.5 per cent in two years is a fairly sharp drop. If the Government were to purchase a greater share in western Canada, that would stimulate the economy and create more jobs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I am pleased my hon. friend raised this. Of course, he is playing with statistics and does not present the true picture. He knows that some very major purchases have been made since we took office, particularly in defence. This includes the frigates, the CF-18, and a number of other defence procurements.
These statistics would skew the total figures. Some of those major contracts which went to the Maritimes, including the Aurora contract and the frigate contracts, will skew the numbers elsewhere.
Let me tell the Hon. Member that I know of companies that never had the opportunity to purchase from the federal Government until we took office. I never saw a Minister of
March 2, 1988

Supply and Services in Cold Lake, Grand Centre or Bonny-ville. 1 never saw him in Vegreville, St. Paul or Fort McMur-ray until this Government took office. When we took office, the Minister of Supply and Services visited the major centres in western Canada to explain how the system worked. People in the West who had the supplies and wanted to do government business did not know how the system worked because they did not have the information.
They never believed they could gain a contract, but let me cite some of the contracts that have been obtained in Alberta that would never have been given without this Government and its purchasing policy.
There is a contract in Vegreville for the supply of an approach system for airports across Canada. Northwest Industries in Edmonton has just been awarded the Hercules aircraft contract. They have been awarded the contract for the repair and maintenance of all Hercules aircraft in Canada. Indeed, that is now spilling over into the United States. You have to look at them in balance. We have more Government purchases going on in western Canada than ever before, and they also have more information out there than ever before.

I was very interested in the Hon. Member's speech when he said working capital is one of the great difficulties for small business. I certainly agree with him. Would he point out to us where in Bill C-113, an Act to promote the development and diversification of the economy of western Canada, to establish the department of western economic diversification and to make consequential amendments to other acts, it provides for working capital for small businesses, especially those in western Canada?
Second, the Hon. Member was outlining the terrible folly of the New Democratic Party in promoting the nationalization of the major oil company. I wonder if the Hon. Member could explain why, in the fall of 1984, shortly after this Government took power, Petro-Canada bought out Gulf Oil, in effect nationalizing it, because it was certainly one of our major oil companies. Why did the Parliamentary Secretary allow that to happen? I have talked to western Canadians who said that at that moment they tore up their Tory card. They could not understand why the Tory Government was nationalizing or taking over Gulf Oil and providing the little easy bump for the production side to go to Reichmanns with a write-off, I understand of about $1 billion. Why would the Government spend $1 billion taking over Gulf Oil when that was clearly different from what the Party had been promising and committing itself to, and what the Hon. Member has spoken against tonight?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an obvious answer and I think the Hon. Member knows it. It is because there was fear it would fall into foreign ownership. It was that simple, I think, at the time.
Western Economic Diversification Act
Let me remind the Hon. Member of the fact that since we took office there has only been one Liberal Member of Parliament representing western Canada. That is the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), the Transport Minister in the previous Government. He is, obviously, a representative of his Party, but he voted against the repeal of the disastrous National Energy Program. He also voted against the repeal of the incremental oil revenue tax from the phase-out of the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax, as agreed by the Western Accord. We are talking about the western representative of the Liberal Party. He has to represent the West as a Liberal. He is the only Liberal from western Canada.
He voted against the increased competition in air and rail transportation, Bill C-18. That was one program western Canada needed. It was one program that got rid of for all times freight rate discrimination. He voted against a $500,000 capital gains exemption for Canadian farmers, Bill C-84. He voted against the expenditure of $92 million for drought relief for western farmers. He voted against providing the Canadian Wheat Board with $200 million to offset its deficit. Perhaps he wanted farmers to make up the difference. At the same time he also voted against funding the development of a new grain transportation method.
He voted against increased foreign investment, the creation of Investment Canada. He voted against increased research, investment in jobs in Canada's pharmaceutical industry. He voted against the settlement of the softwood lumber dispute that had been negotiated at the request of the producing provinces, western provinces. He voted against legislation which compensated the uninsured depositors of two western banks. He did this in spite of the fact that the depositors of those banks included many municipalities, educational institutions, credit unions and school boards. He voted against $17 million of Atlantic fisheries restructuring, he voted against providing the Cape Breton Development Corporation with an extra $7 million for the modernization of the railway operation. He voted against increasing the total amount of money that may be loaned under the Small Businesses Loans Act. Where is the Liberal Party coming from? The Hon. Member for Algoma has the gall to stand in this House and ask questions when tied around his neck is a millstone in the form of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, who is supposed to represent western Canada. I cannot believe it.

speechtext: No, 1 will not.

That figures. He is a good hit and run artist.
I have been through this diversification thing for the umpteenth time, ever since I was a kid in the dirty thirties. I heard about it with respect to western Canada and Atlantic Canada. I heard about it with respect to the North and northern Ontario, the divisions of the North, the Roads to Resources.
We have had nothing but Grits and Tories in Government for 125 years. R. B. Bennett was going to blast us into the world markets. He was going to diversify the economy.
He did blast us!

We got blasted all right, on to $5 per month relief. Then we got the Liberals. The war saved us for a while. After the war the Liberals said that they would diversify and that they would get us into the world markets. "We have to diversify", they told us. The only thing that saved R. B. Bennett was that he told us to diversify out west, which we did, and then it did not rain. So we got dried out.
The Liberals came along then and said: "We have to diversify". Again, the people out west believed them and they diversified. We were up to our eyeballs in grain. We had a glut that some would not believe. Our people out west diversified into livestock of all types, poultry and even bee keeping. A whole bunch of little businesses started up, plants and whatnot, to build feed bins and to help construct feedlots, et cetera. We then diversified all over the place. Grain prices were cheap. One could buy three bushels of barley for $1. At that price one could afford to feed cattle.
So we went into cattle and hogs. We raised so many cattle and hogs that two things happened. First, the Americans slapped an embargo on us because we were sending too many down there. Second, the price dropped to less than it cost for a bushel of barley. We have been through that one, too. This was in the 1950s and the 1960s.
Then we got to the 1960s and the 1970s. We had mostly Liberal Governments. We had Tories right up until 1979, including 1979, who talked about diversification.
We decided that in order to diversify we would grow all this rapeseed which is now called Canola and make vegetable oil out of it. We built about eight plants in western Canada as part of diversification. We quit growing so darn much wheat and so darn much cattle, hogs and chickens.
We just got into the diversification plan for the fourteenth time in the last hundred years and what happened? The Government decided to give tens of millions of dollars to oilseed processing plants. Where? In southern Ontario. What did they process? Soybeans from the United States. Of the eight plants that we used to have in western Canada there are now two left. So much for that episode of diversification.
Mr. Speaker, please forgive me for feeling a bit of cynicism.
I do not like being a cynic. It is the last resort of the guy who gave up. One can hardly blame me for saying: "Again?" Unless and until a national Government, whether it be made up of Conservatives, Liberals or NDPers, decides to get together with the business community, the trade union movement and the agricultural community to have a planned economy and direct the location of industry and provide it with an equality of opportunity to compete in the markets in central

Canada and outside Canada, then diversification plans for Atlantic Canada or western Canada will go down the drain just like all the other ones have before. We have been through this innumerable times.
It means that we have to say to central Canada, and I am sure that there are people in Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa who will agree, that those places do not need to get any bigger. They cannot even keep up with their housing requirements and the municipal facilities that their people and industry need. They are way behind. They cannot even get rid of all their garbage.
The next time an industry wants to start up it should be provided with the capacity to go into business in Atlantic Canada or western Canada and be able to present its production in the markets of central Canada or anywhere else in the world in equal competition with those which make the same products. Let me give Hon. Members an illustration of that point.
We used to ship 10 to 12 train loads of western coal a day from Saskatchewan, Alberta and eastern British Columbia to central Canada for heating and for the production of electricity. What has happened since then? We keep raising Cain in the House time and time again about acid rain which is caused by high-sulphur coal, brought in from where? The United States. If this western diversification plan worked to do anything, it would provide an equity of transportation costs. We would move western coal to the tune of 10, 12 or 15 train loads a day, even if it was only as far as Thunder Bay. We could then ship it by water through the Seaway to all the power plants, particularly those of Ontario Hydro. Yet here we sit. We are up to here in coal in the three most western provinces. It is low-sulphur coal which would do more to reduce the production of acid rain inside Canada than anything else. The problem is that under the free trade agreement, the Americans would not like that because a statutory coal rate would be needed, just like a statutory grain rate.
We can talk all we like about whether it is $200 million per year or $1 billion per year for the next five years. Unless we reorder the location, the production, the manufacturing and the processing of our products and resources, they will fail. We have been through this several times before.
I am several times bitten; I am more times shy. At the moment we have an excellent poultry producer in Wynyard, Saskatchewan. He diversified. He has hundreds of thousands of dollars invested in that plant. He received some grants from the federal and provincial Governments. He produces marvellous roasting chickens. One can go to the Safeway or the Coop in Regina to buy them. They are beautiful. The problem is that he diversified. The same stores are selling chickens produced in Georgia-
