Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before I was so rudely interrupted, we have been through this diversification bit before. The thrust of a national Government's policy, of any of the three political Parties in this place, has to be the reordering of our economy and the reordering of the location of the production of that economy. Without that, eastern, western or northern diversification programs are doomed to fail. We have tried them many times before. If we are going to do what the Government states that it wants to do, then it has to face up to the fact that the free trade deal goes down the drain. Everything that the federal Government in co-operation with the provinces tries to do will be deemed by the Americans to be a subsidy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Baloney!

Well, they have already done it, they are doing it now, and they will continue to do it.
Members of the U.S. administration, the U.S. Congress, state governors and legislatures are already accusing us of subsidies on programs that national governments, be they Liberal or Conservative, designed to assist in regional development. That is the reality that this Government or any other Party that forms the Government of Canada will have to face up to.
In order to make a regional development program succeed, the Government of this country, of any political stripe, has to make a decision not to discriminate against any other region, not to discriminate against any other country, but to discriminate in favour of an underdeveloped region. Discrimination for rather than discrimination against is 100 per cent different.

March 2, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
For a regional development fund to be effective, whether it is in western Canada or Atlantic Canada, we have to take into account our geography, our climate, and the distances we have to face to get our production into the market-places in central Canada, or anywhere else in the world. To attempt to do anything other than that is doomed to failure.
The problem with the Conservatives and Liberals is that they have never learned from their own history, and they are attempting to repeat it. If they wish to do things about western development, my good friend, the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) and I will have to persuade the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski), the Cabinet, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to complete the rehabilitation of railway lines. If any self-respecting investor wants to build a plant, he is not going to do it in Assiniboia, Weyburn, Moose Jaw, or in any other place where there is no railway line. The Government has reneged on the rehabilitation of railway lines to the tune of something in the order of $138 million. That is how far behind we are, and there is this year and next year left.
The Hon. Member for Assiniboia and I have tried our best. We have had some modest success, last minute changes of heart by the bureaucrats in the Department of Transport, and maybe with the Minister of Transport.
Surely that is the type of investment that pays off for western Canada. I find it appalling when Conservatives talk to me about having a government run by sound business practices, when two or three years ago it sunk $10 million into a branch line 77 miles long and refuses to finish the job, which will take another $13 million. That is in the Bengough subdivision in my hon. friend's riding. The Hon. Member and I have both been fighting to get that done. The way it sits now is that this Government, with all its western diversification plans, will let that $10 million that has already been spent go down the drain, just throw it out. The other $13 million has to be spent to finish the rehabilitation of that railway line, or $10 million will be totally wasted. That job has to be done. It requires $138 million between now and the end of November, 1989. The rail line rehabilitation alone is half of what the Government proposes to spend in each year for five years.
If they want to do some things for western Canada, why don't they finish what has been started? The Liberals started this particular project, but why does the Government not finish what it states is a good idea before starting into other things? It does not have the slightest idea in what direction to go.
One cannot diversify. There cannot be a champagne production and a champagne economy in a beer market. The beer market is the small market of western Canada. I consider western Canada anywhere from Sudbury west. I consider eastern Canada from Quebec City east, and all of northern Quebec. Unless we reorder, we say to industry and the market in central Canada that we will lay down production, manufacturing, and service materials from western Canada and Atlantic Canada. We will lay it down in the market in central Canada, in the United States, or anywhere else in the world, at a price that you will have to compete with in terms of quality, quantity, delivery, warrantys, and everything else, but the cost of getting it there will be equal.
Surely that is fair. Surely that takes into account our geography. If the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) had $500 million that he did not know what to do with, he would be stupid to invest it in some kind of a manufacturing or processing plant with western Canada or Atlantic Canada in the type of conditions and economy that we presently have. It would be dumb. If he went for a banker to a loan, he would be laughed out of the place.
A planned economy requires a reordering of the location of our productive capacity, whether it is in manufactured goods or in agricultural processing. There is more to Canada than Montreal, Ottawa, and Toronto. They do not need any more. They cannot handle all they have now. That is what we have to do, no matter what Party is in government.
I wish to assure the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), when this Bill is called for debate, that I will be here to participate in the 10-minute question and answer period.
